descs.en: A trauma surgeon reborn as a governor’s daughter falls for the Emperor’s nephew from a balcony — and then does something very foolish to see him again. A slow, warm historical romance told in stitches, letters and one river.

chapters.title: The Girl on the Balcony
chapters.desc: A general rides through Qingzhou, and a sixteen-year-old with a surgeon’s memory forgets to breathe.
chapters.epigraph: “Come away from there. It is unbecoming to stare at soldiers.” “I’m observing the botanical garden, Mother.” “From memory?”
chapters.content:
The spring rains had stopped two days ago, and Qingzhou smelled of wet stone and fresh herbs — which Yun Shiyu had decided, over sixteen years, was the closest this era came to the clean antiseptic scent she still sometimes dreamed of. She was on the second-floor balcony of the governor’s residence, elbows on the carved railing, pretending to study the herb garden below. She wasn’t studying the herb garden. She was watching the street.

The servants had started it, really. That morning, the household had begun humming with quiet excitement — whispered conversations, Cook dispatching her assistant for extra provisions, the head housekeeper instructing the lower maids to ensure the front gate was presentable. Shiyu had set down her father’s worn copy of the Shennong Bencao Jing and paid careful attention. A military procession. A young general returning from the north, travelling through Qingzhou on his way to the capital. The Emperor’s own nephew, no less. He had just resolved a border campaign in a single season that lesser commanders took years to finish.

“Cold as mountain ice. The men follow him like he was born to command.” Cook’s assistant had breathed to one of the maids, their voices carrying perfectly well to the study.

Shiyu absorbed this with the part of her mind that was still, even after eleven years in this body, a trauma physician categorizing incoming information. Young. Orphaned early. Rapid military success at an age when most men were still finding their footing. She had stopped herself there. Even her internal monologue could become uncomfortably clinical, and she was reasonably certain that no other sixteen-year-old girl in Qingzhou was constructing psychological profiles of military generals as a hobby.

She was, she told herself, simply curious.

“Shiyu, come away from there. It is unbecoming to stare at soldiers,” her mother called from inside.

“I’m observing the botanical garden, Mother.”

“The botanical garden is on the south side of the house.”

“I’m observing it from memory.”

She heard her mother’s footsteps retreat towards the interior rooms, accompanied by quiet muttering about daughters who had inherited too many of their father’s odd habits. Shiyu allowed herself a small smile and returned to the street. She saw him before she understood what she was seeing. He rode a black horse of visible quality, and he moved with the stillness of a man completely at home with authority — not performing it, simply inhabited by it. His armour was black with silver edging, without the gold embellishment the provincial officials favoured. His helmet was carried at his side rather than worn. He was speaking to someone beside him, and even from the balcony above she could see the economy of it — a few words, the other person nodding twice, withdrawing. Whatever had been communicated took perhaps the space of a breath and was entirely sufficient.

Her father’s greeting party emerged from the front gate, and the General turned his head to receive it. His face was visible from where she stood. Shiyu had been a physician in her previous life. She had seen a great many faces and had cultivated the professional habit of observing them without being startled by them. She wasn’t, she had always told herself, susceptible. She was startled. He was striking, in the way that sharp things were striking, commanding attention through precision rather than softness, but what startled her was the totality of him: the line of his jaw, the dark eyes that swept her father’s greeting with an assessment so brief and complete she felt it from above. Neither warm nor cold. Simply exact. He nodded once to her father — correct, measured, neither more nor less than the situation required — and his gaze moved on.

It didn’t reach the balcony. He wasn’t looking at her. She was aware, in a remote and deeply inconvenient way, that her heart was doing something medically uninteresting and personally significant. She straightened away from the railing and pressed the back of her hand briefly to her cheek. Warm. Yes.

“Purely academic,” she said to no one.

The procession moved on. The street returned to its ordinary life. And Shiyu stood on the balcony for a long while longer than necessary, watching the empty road, her usually reliable internal monologue entirely, unusually quiet.

chapters.title: The Return of Uncle Xiang
chapters.desc: Her uncle, the army’s chief physician, comes home for a few days, and she asks all the wrong questions.
chapters.epigraph: “He has declined every proposal put to him. Why do you ask, Shiyu?” “I was thinking about military logistics.”
chapters.content:
Uncle Xiang arrived twelve days later, as he always did — without advance notice, with a great deal of energy, and smelling of the medicinal smoke that Shiyu associated with field medicine and long roads. Yun Xiangyi was forty-eight years old, lean and purposeful in the way of men who had spent decades moving between encampments and thinking hard about difficult problems. He was her father’s younger brother, though the two men had taken such different paths from the same origin that visitors sometimes had trouble believing it. Her father, Yun Chengde, had grown soft and comfortable in his role as governor — not lazily, but gently, the way a good man with a peaceful life naturally settled. Her uncle had stayed honed, sharpened by his years of service to the northern army.

The household welcomed him with the warm chaos that always attended his returns. Her mother fussed about whether he had eaten. He hadn’t, properly, which was entirely predictable and which he dismissed with the good-natured deflection of a man who had been receiving this concern for two decades. Her father emerged from his study with a medical text still in hand, and the two brothers embraced with the easy warmth of men who had never needed to perform affection.

Shiyu waited. She served tea. She listened. She refilled cups when they needed refilling. She was the picture of a dutiful niece, and she was simultaneously calculating the optimal moment to ask a question she had been constructing for eleven days. That moment arrived when her mother went to speak with Cook and her father became absorbed in a mild debate about an herbal compound. Shiyu set down her teacup.

“Uncle. The general’s procession passed through twelve days ago. You serve his army — General Zhan Lingyun. You’ve been with his command for eight years, haven’t you?” she said, keeping her voice easy.

“About that,” her uncle said, not looking up from the text.

“He must be demanding. To have built such a reputation at twenty-five.”

“Precise is the better word. He expects the same standard from everyone that he holds himself to. His men follow him because they trust him, not because they fear him. The distinction matters,” Uncle Xiang said, with the tone of someone choosing language carefully.

Shiyu nodded. Reasonable leader. Clear standards. The kind of commander whose men reported genuine loyalty rather than performed compliance.

“Is he —” she began, then reconsidered.

She started again, very carefully.

“I imagine someone in his position receives a great many marriage proposals from the capital’s noble families.”

The page-turning stopped. She felt rather than saw her uncle look up. She kept her eyes on her folded hands, her expression arranged into something she hoped read as idle observation rather than the pointed inquiry it absolutely was.

“He has declined every proposal put to him. The Emperor does not press the matter. Why do you ask, Shiyu?” Uncle Xiang said, in the voice of a man who had noticed something and was deciding what to do with the noticing.

“I was thinking about military logistics. Whether commanders without family obligations in the capital tend to maintain more consistent field presence. It is a medical consideration —” she said, which was partially true.

“Shiyu.”

His voice was gentle. Entirely, infuriatingly gentle, in the way of someone who saw considerably more than he was acknowledging. She looked up. He was watching her with the expression she privately thought of as his diagnostic face — the one he wore when a patient’s description didn’t match the condition they believed they had.

“What?” she said, hoping she sounded more innocent than she felt.

“Nothing,” he said, after a moment, and returned to the text.

At the edge of her vision she saw him and her father exchange a glance — the brief, knowing communication of two men who had been watching an unusual daughter and niece for sixteen years and had long since learned to read the shape of her misdirections. Warmth rose in her cheeks. She fixed her gaze on her teacup. She spent the rest of the evening behaving with impeccable propriety and trying very hard not to think about dark eyes and the economy of a single correct nod.

She succeeded intermittently. Before she retired, she paused in the corridor outside her uncle’s room. His door was slightly open.

“Uncle. When do you return to the camp?” she said through the gap.

A brief silence. “Perhaps two to three weeks. Why?”

“No particular reason. Good night, Uncle,” she said.

“Good night, Shiyu.”

She went to her room and lay on her sleeping mat staring at the painted ceiling for quite a long time before she finally slept. Two to three weeks.

In the morning, she resolved, she would be entirely sensible about this.

chapters.title: The Decision
chapters.desc: There is no sensible way to see him again. So she picks a foolish one.
chapters.epigraph: “I understand what you’re asking. And the answer is no.” — Uncle Xiang, the first time
chapters.content:
She wasn’t, in the morning, entirely sensible. It took her four days to reach the decision and seven drafts to write the letter. The decision was this: she was going to the camp. The letter was for her parents, to be found after she left, written honest enough not to feel like a lie but not so alarming that it would send soldiers galloping after her before she had even arrived.

She had tried the direct approach first. She had made a well-reasoned appeal to her father, during the after-dinner hour when he was most relaxed, framed around the genuine medical and professional merits of studying army medicine firsthand: the volume of injury cases, the systematic approach her uncle had developed, the practical knowledge that simply didn’t exist in civilian Qingzhou.

Her father had listened to every word with the patient attention he always gave her, which was one of the things she loved most about him. Then he had said, very gently: “No.”

She had tried her uncle next. He had listened for the space of ten breaths before stopping her with a raised hand. “I understand what you’re asking. And the answer is no. A military camp is not appropriate for an unmarried girl from a respectable family, regardless of the medical justification,” he said.

She had let the matter rest for four days, during which she was cooperative and cheerful and showed absolutely no visible signs of planning anything. She helped with household accounts. She assisted her father with his administrative reports as promised. She discussed medical texts with her uncle in the evenings with the pleasant, unfocused enthusiasm of someone who had accepted her circumstances and moved on. She had also, during those four days, packed a small bundle.

She wasn’t proud of this. She was also committed to it. She had identified the medical supply carriage that would leave before dawn on the fourth day, noted the storage compartment beneath its main body, and calculated that the journey to the camp would take several days — long enough to make returning her more trouble than letting her stay. She was aware this was optimistic reasoning. She packed the bundle anyway.

At the hour before dawn she made her way to the supply carriage and climbed in. The thing about being a physician, even one eleven years removed from her original context, was that she had a pragmatic relationship with discomfort. She had endured call rooms and forty-minute crouches under supply cabinets. She wasn’t a woman who found small enclosed spaces unbearable. She revised this assessment after approximately four hours inside the storage compartment.

The smell of preserved medicines was overwhelming. The road was significantly less smooth than it appeared from the outside. The darkness was total except for thin lines of light through the wooden seams — enough to see by in a technical sense, not enough to read, which gave her far more time to think than she wanted. She didn’t turn back. She heard her uncle’s voice once, outside, conferring with someone about the supply inventory, and she held herself completely still, barely breathing. The compartment door wasn’t tested. The carriage moved on.

She arrived thinking about three things: that the plan had been objectively foolish from the beginning, that she had committed to it and would see it through, and that whatever came next — and she wasn’t naive about how next would likely begin — she had chosen it. The rest, she supposed, was up to him.

chapters.title: Discovered
chapters.desc: Four hours hidden in a supply carriage, and then the lid comes off.
chapters.epigraph: “She concealed herself before departure, General.” “In whose carriage?” “…Yours.”
chapters.content:
The storage compartment opened at the frontier checkpoint — not by her choice, but by the hands of a young soldier conducting inventory — and she found herself looking into the frankly astounded face of a man who couldn’t have been much older than nineteen. He stared at her. She stared back.

“There’s —” he began.

“I can explain,” she said, which wasn’t entirely true but was the only available response.

“There is a girl in the General’s supply carriage,” he finished, looking over his shoulder at his companion.

Her uncle arrived at something close to a run. His face carried not anger but a very controlled stillness — the face he wore over patients with serious complications, not the face she had ever wanted directed at herself.

“Shiyu,” he said. Just her name. In that tone.

She had straightened herself as best she could in the circumstances, clasped her hands, and met his eyes, because looking away would have been worse. There was a bruise forming on her elbow. Her legs felt unsteady. She smelled strongly of medicinal herbs in a way that wasn’t how she had imagined this going.

“Uncle. I’m sorry for the manner of my arrival. I can explain my reasoning —”

“Not here. Not now.” A word sent the gathered soldiers back to their duties. A second word sent someone ahead with a message.

She understood from the direction that message went that they were being summoned.

“The General wants to speak with you. Both of us. Now,” her uncle said, and something in his voice told her this had been inevitable from the moment she was found.

They walked across the camp together. She had been here for barely the time it takes to drink a cup of tea and she was already aware of being assessed — not the curious glances of Qingzhou, but the trained surveillance of an environment where every anomaly was automatically evaluated as a potential problem. She was an anomaly. She kept her chin level and her hands steady. The command tent was large and practical, lit by oil lamps even in daylight. Maps on the central table. Nothing unnecessary, nothing decorative. She registered all of this in the brief moment before she registered the man seated at the far end.

General Zhan Lingyun. He was entirely different from the impression on the balcony, and exactly as she remembered. The distance of the street below had flattened him into something striking but contained. Here, in this tent, there was no distance. The full weight of his presence was immediate, and considerable, and not at all flattened. He was in the formal inner tunic of an officer at rest — black, silver detailing at collar and cuffs. His posture in the chair was the posture of someone who didn’t need to perform authority because he simply had it. His dark eyes directed towards her with an attention that was assessing and absolutely flat, evaluating her the way he might evaluate an unexpected development in a campaign: neither hostile nor welcoming, simply determining what needed to be done.

She was very glad she had the habit of keeping her face composed. She was less glad that warmth was rising to her cheeks despite every professional instinct she possessed, which was entirely physiological and completely unhelpful and there was nothing she could do about it. She bowed. Properly, at the depth appropriate to his rank and her current position, which was very low by any measure.

“Chief Physician Yun. Who is this,” the General said. His voice was exactly what she had known it would be — calm, measured, the kind that carried without effort.

“My niece, General. Yun Shiyu. Daughter of the Governor of Qingzhou. She concealed herself in the medical supply carriage without my knowledge. I take full responsibility.”

“How did she come to be there.”

“She concealed herself before departure, General.”

A silence. She kept her eyes at the appropriate angle — not floor-gazing, not presumptuous eye contact, the neutral space between.

“Raise your head,” the General said.

She did.

He studied her for a moment. “Your name.”

“Yun Shiyu.” Her voice came out steady. She was grateful for this.

“Why.”

She had prepared for this question. She had spent four days preparing precisely how to answer it. She had the layered explanation ready — genuine academic interest in military medicine, the educational resources unavailable in civilian practice, her uncle’s expertise as justification. She said it.

“You had no other way because you had been refused permission,” he said.

“Yes, General.”

He stood — efficient, untroubled — and walked to the far end of the tent to speak with an officer. She stood with her hands clasped and tried to control her breathing, and thought with considerable clarity that she was in a very significant amount of trouble.

chapters.title: The Interrogation and the Truth
chapters.desc: Accused of being a spy, she has one defence left: the embarrassing truth.
chapters.epigraph: “The enemy’s intelligence assets always say that.” “Do they also say they came to look at you?”
chapters.content:
They came in from the sides of the tent. She hadn’t seen them enter. Five officers, present, and the quality of their attention was entirely different from anything she had experienced before — this wasn’t the curious surveillance of a city that found her odd. This was the trained, professional assessment of people whose function was to identify threats, and they were looking at her like one.

The broadest stepped forward first — the scarred man, his left cheek bearing a long old wound. He considered her the way she imagined he considered a fortification wall he had been assigned to breach.

“A governor’s daughter. In the General’s personal supply carriage. Travelling with the military column. Without authorisation, without escort, without documentation. That is not curiosity. That is an operation,” he said, to no one and everyone. He let this sit.

“I am not —” she began.

He said, “You concealed yourself. Deliberately. For days. You waited until the camp before revealing yourself, which means you knew exactly where you were going and chose not to be found until arrival. That is not a girl who snuck out of her house on a whim. That is someone who planned this.”

The slighter man — scholar’s bearing, ink-stained fingers unusual on a military man — spoke from her left, his voice precise and entirely without heat: “We are currently at war with a border faction whose intelligence network has been attempting to embed assets within the army’s medical staff for the past two years. You arrived in the medical supply compartment. You carry medical equipment. You have some level of training. The coincidence is notable.”

The word spy wasn’t spoken. It didn’t need to be. It was in the room like smoke. Shiyu felt the cold of genuine fear — not the social embarrassment she had been managing since discovery but something much more serious. She was acutely aware of how this looked. How it had to look. How she would have looked at it, if she had been on the other side of the situation.

“I am not a spy. I have no connection to —” she said.

“The enemy’s intelligence assets always say that. We would not be doing our job if we took your word for it,” Wei Tiecheng said, not unkindly, in the tone of a man stating a fact.

The young officer at the entrance — the one she had noticed was sharper than he looked — said: “Her uncle vouches for her identity. The governor of Qingzhou is a known and trusted figure. But a trusted figure can have a compromised household without knowing it. And an intelligent operation would absolutely use the niece of the army’s own Chief Physician. The access alone —”

“I am not, a spy,” Shiyu said, with more force than she had managed yet.

“Then explain what you actually are. Because what you have given us so far — a desire to study military medicine — does not explain the concealment, the timing, or the fact that you have no letter of introduction, no formal request, no documentation of any kind. A girl who wanted medical training would have applied through her uncle in writing. You didn’t. You hid. Which means you knew the legitimate path would not give you what you wanted,” Lin Wenyuan said, still precise, still without heat.

He folded his hands.

“What did you want?”

The silence after this question had a particular quality. They were all looking at her. Her uncle was beside her with the expression of a man who had gone very quiet and was waiting, and she understood that even he didn’t know what she was going to say — that the real answer, the one she had never said out loud to anyone, was about to have its first encounter with open air.

She could still manage this. She had prepared answers. She could say: I was desperate for real medical experience. She could say: I knew my uncle would refuse if asked directly. She could construct any number of reasonable explanations that were adjacent to the truth without being the truth. She looked up. The General was watching her from his chair with those dark eyes, and the quality of his watching was entirely different from the others. They were waiting to assess her answer. He was waiting to see whether she would tell the truth.

She understood this clearly. She didn’t know how she understood it. But she did. And she understood, looking at him, that a lie would work on the others — she was clever enough, and the lie was good enough, and they were operating from a security framework that was logical but wasn’t aimed at her actual situation. A lie would probably get her sent home with a reprimand rather than treated as a genuine threat.

But a lie wouldn’t work on him. Not because he would necessarily detect it. Because he would know she had chosen it. She breathed. The scaffolding of her prepared explanations came down.

“I wanted to see the General again,” she said.

The silence that followed was a completely different kind of silence from all the ones before it.

“His procession passed through Qingzhou. I saw him from the balcony of my father’s residence. I had never — I did not know that a person could see someone once and then spend eleven days being unable to stop thinking about them. I asked my uncle about him. I asked — inappropriate questions, the kind that made my uncle look at me with his diagnostic face, and my father look at the ceiling, and I understood what I felt but I had no idea what to do with it because it was — It was not going away. Every sensible thing I told myself made no difference. So I made a plan. Which was not a good plan. I understand, now, why it was not a good plan. But I am not a spy. I am a sixteen-year-old girl who made a profoundly impractical decision because she could not think of a better one,” she said, because she had started and she could hear how this sounded and she needed to get all of it out before she lost the courage for any of it. She stopped. Drew breath.

She stopped. The tent was absolutely silent. Wei Tiecheng’s mouth was slightly open. He closed it. Lin Wenyuan was looking at her with an expression she couldn’t catalogue — the expression of a man whose logical framework had just been handed something it hadn’t modelled for. Lü Yue, at the tent’s far wall, had the look of a senior officer confronting a situation his experience hadn’t prepared him for.

Zhou Hua made a small sound that was immediately and completely suppressed. Chen Ye, at the entrance, had gone very still in the way she would later come to recognise as him suppressing an expression with every professional tool he possessed. Her uncle made a quiet exhale — not words, the sound of a man who had suspected something and had received it confirmed in a manner substantially more direct than anticipated.

And the General —she looked at him. He was watching her with an expression she couldn’t read. Neither anger nor contempt, but something more complex: a quality of genuine surprise, very carefully controlled, as though he were keeping it from occupying more of his face than he intended. It was the first unguarded thing she had seen from him, and it lasted perhaps three heartbeats before the careful neutrality returned.

Three heartbeats. Long enough. He stood.

“Chief Physician Yun. Your niece will remain in the medical tent. She will be understood by the camp to have arrived as part of the medical staff rotation from the capital. Everyone in this tent will maintain that account.”

“Yes, General.”

“The girl is here. Returning her immediately creates more complications for her family than a supervised stay will. She will assist the Chief Physician and conduct herself appropriately. You came here for medical knowledge. That is what you will be here for, and it is the only thing. You will not approach the command area without a direct summons. You will not create difficulty for your uncle. You will conduct yourself correctly and in six weeks you will return to Qingzhou with work worth having done. Do you understand.” He looked at her, and his voice was flat and clear and entirely without warmth.

“Yes, General,” she said. Her voice was very small.

“Good.”

He turned back to the maps. Her uncle’s hand came to rest on her shoulder. She went.

In the afternoon air outside the command tent she stopped walking and stood with the camp activity moving around her, indifferent to everything that had just happened, and she thought about those three unguarded heartbeats, and she thought about the fact that she was still here, not on a carriage back to Qingzhou, and she thought about what it was going to cost her to conduct herself correctly for six weeks in a camp that contained him.

Considerable, she decided. It was going to cost her considerable. She pressed her fingers briefly to her warm cheeks, breathed the unfamiliar smell of the northern frontier, and followed her uncle towards the medical tent. She had six weeks. She would be excellent at the medicine. She would try very hard at the rest.

chapters.title: The Medical Tent
chapters.desc: Six weeks, a tent full of wounded men, and a chance to prove she belongs.
chapters.epigraph: “Every case is documented. The General requires it, reviews it, and uses it. It is not optional.” — Uncle Xiang
chapters.content:
The medical tent was large, divided into three clear sections — examination and treatment at the front, supply storage and preparation in the middle, sleeping quarters at the back. Everything organised with a precision she recognised as her uncle’s hand: labelled, categorized, the same systematic logic she had observed in his visits home, applied here on a larger scale with the additional discipline of military need. She stood at the entrance with her small bundle in her arms and tried to look as though she hadn’t just confessed her feelings to a general in front of his entire senior command staff.

Her uncle came to stand beside her. He didn’t speak immediately. This was, she had learned over eleven years, the most significant form of his displeasure — not raised voices, not harsh reprimands, just the silence that communicated the full weight of everything he wasn’t saying, and let that weight do the work. She waited.

“Your sleeping space is at the back. You will wear the assistant’s uniform at all times while working. It marks you as medical staff and nothing else. Anyone who asks has been told you are a physician’s assistant from the capital. You will not volunteer anything beyond that,” he said at last.

“Yes, Uncle.”

“The work begins at dawn. Every case is documented. The General requires it, reviews it, and uses it to improve health management across the whole camp. It is meticulous work and it is not optional.”

He handed her the case records from the overnight watch. She read them in the growing lamplight and began. She hadn’t fully understood, when her uncle warned her about the documentation system, quite how much of a military physician’s day was composed of writing things down. Every patient, every complaint, every herb prepared, every bandage changed, every follow-up observation. The format was strict, the language precise, the standard for completeness unforgiving.

The first time she submitted a report her uncle deemed insufficiently detailed, he handed it back without a word and pointed to a section she had summarised where he required full description. She rewrote it. The second time — a straightforward recovery report she had felt was entirely adequate — he explained, in the careful tone he used for genuine teaching, that conclusions without supporting observations were opinions, and opinions weren’t evidence. She rewrote that one too.

By the end of the first week, her reports were thorough, structured, and reviewed without being returned. She took this as the highest available praise. She didn’t see the General. This was, she told herself, exactly as it should be. He had given her clear instructions. She was following them. Their paths had no natural intersection and she wasn’t creating artificial ones. She was being exactly what she had been told to be.

She was also, privately, aware of this fact at approximately every other moment of every day. She heard about him through the camp’s ordinary noise — soldiers talking during treatments, her uncle’s brief references in medical context. On the fourth day, carrying linens to the drying racks along the camp’s western supply path, she saw him. He was walking with the Vice-Commander towards the training ground, both men in discussion, and he didn’t look towards the supply path. He was listening, his hands at his back, posture easy, entirely occupied with the conversation.

She kept walking. She didn’t slow down. She fixed her eyes on the drying racks ahead and thought, with clinical precision, about the optimal temperature for drying wound dressings and whether the afternoon wind was suitable. She also, in the portion of her mind that hadn’t received the clinical-precision instructions, felt her heart do the same irrational thing it had done on the balcony in Qingzhou. She hung the linens. She walked back. She wrote an excellent report that evening and noted three contributing factors to a soldier’s improving shoulder mobility with full supporting observations.

This was the shape of the first week.

chapters.title: He Reads the Reports
chapters.desc: Chen Ye lets slip what the General does with her reports in the evenings.
chapters.epigraph: “The reports, certainly. The Chief Physician mentioned they were unusually thorough.” — Chen Ye, choosing his words
chapters.content:
By the second week, she had learned the camp’s geography well enough to understand, without being told, which routes passed near the command area. She told herself she wasn’t using this knowledge. She was, occasionally, using this knowledge. There were two wells. The northern well was closer — forty paces from the medical tent. The southern well was further, perhaps a hundred and sixty paces, and the route to it passed along the western edge of the command area. She used the northern well for everything urgent. For the less urgent water needs she found herself, most mornings, taking the longer route. The bucket was heavy enough to justify the effort. The morning air was pleasant.

She walked past with the deliberate stride of someone going somewhere purposeful, and she didn’t look directly at the command tent, and she didn’t slow her pace. She also didn’t see him. The tent showed activity — couriers, sounds of discussion — but never him. She kept doing the walks anyway. She wasn’t entirely able to explain this, even to herself.

On the ninth day, Chen Ye appeared at the medical tent to collect the General’s personal medical supplies. He watched her work with the relaxed attention of someone in no particular hurry.

“You’ve settled in well,” he said.

“The work is good,” she replied.

“The reports, certainly. The Chief Physician mentioned they were unusually thorough. The morning water runs are also a consistent feature of your routine, I’ve noticed.”

Her hands didn’t stop moving. “The southern well produces cleaner water for medical preparation. The northern well sits closer to the stable drainage. A minor difference, but worth considering for wound care,” she said, with the careful neutrality of someone delivering a prepared answer.

A silence.

“Of course, very thorough,” Chen Ye said, with the tone of a man finding an explanation entirely reasonable and also completely transparent, and deciding — for reasons of his own — not to press it.

He accepted the completed supply package and moved towards the exit. At the entrance he paused — this was, she was already understanding, a habit of his — and said, without turning around, “He reads the medical reports, you know. All of them. In the evenings. The extended observations particularly — the ones where she tracked how men recovered and what they had been eating. He annotates them.”

She looked up. But Chen Ye had already left. She stood alone in the supply section for a moment with a box of dried herbs in her hands, feeling something move in her chest that she wasn’t going to name. She set down the herbs. She went back to work.

That evening, writing her report by lamplight, she was more thorough than usual. More detailed in the analysis, more precise in the conclusions. Not because she was trying to impress anyone — purely on principle. If someone was reading with enough care to annotate, the work deserved to be as good as she could make it. She didn’t think about dark eyes reading her words in the lamplight of the command tent.

Not much. The next morning she took the longer route to the southern well.

chapters.title: The Battle, and What Came After
chapters.desc: The eastern flank breaks, and the tent fills faster than she can count.
chapters.epigraph: “Go directly there and directly back. I will know if you don’t.” “I know you will.”
chapters.content:
The messenger came at midday, riding hard enough that she heard the hooves before she saw the dust. She was grinding a compound preparation when the sound reached the tent. The kind of hoofbeats with a different quality from ordinary camp movement — faster and sustained and purposeful in a way that made soldiers in earshot straighten before they had consciously registered why. She set down her pestle. Her uncle was already at the entrance.

Eastern flank. Cavalry engagement. The General moving with the main force. Casualties imminent. Her uncle turned. His face had changed — the warmth gone entirely, replaced by absolute focus. This was the Chief Military Physician, not her uncle. Not the man she had grown up with.

“We prepare now. Everything. Maximum capacity. I need every surface cleared, every supply accessible. You know the system — act on it. If you don’t know, make the more conservative choice and tell me after.”

“Understood,” she said, and she was already moving.

What followed was five hours she would carry for the rest of her life. They came in waves. First the walking wounded — she triaged with her uncle’s system, serious risk of deterioration first, stable cases assigned to wait. She cleaned wounds and stitched closures and applied the salt-water solution and splinted a fracture with the calm efficiency of someone who had set bones before, talking the patient through the pain with the low, steady voice she had developed for exactly this purpose. She didn’t have time to be afraid. She simply worked, the way she had worked in the trauma ward in the life she still remembered — one patient, then the next, then the next.

Her uncle summoned her at the height of the crisis to handle two cases simultaneously — one soldier with an arterial nick that required delicate management, one with a chest wound she had to assess for internal involvement. She handled both. She didn’t think about whether she was capable while she was doing it. She only thought about it afterward, when the tent had quieted and her hands were still and the weight of what had just happened settled onto her chest.

She was still writing her notes from the third-to-last case when her uncle appeared at the documentation surface and said, without preamble: “The General has been hit. Arrow wound, upper arm. I cannot leave.”

She was very careful about her face. She said, “I can attend him. Arrow wound, upper arm — I’ve treated two today of the same type. The procedure is straightforward. Your skills are needed here.”

Her uncle looked at her. She met his gaze and kept her expression professional, which required more effort in that moment than almost anything she had done all day.

“Go directly there and directly back. You will treat the wound and only the wound. You will conduct yourself with complete propriety,” he said.

“Yes, Uncle.”

“I will know if you don’t.”

“I know you will.”

She gathered her supplies with hands that were steadier than she expected them to be, and followed the soldier out of the medical tent towards the command area.

chapters.title: The Arrow and the Heartbeat
chapters.desc: She stitches the General’s arm, and her hands are steadier than her heart.
chapters.epigraph: “Is it just me, or did the General not take his eyes off her the entire time?” — overheard, outside the command tent
chapters.content:
He was standing. She had half-expected him to be seated — most patients with blood loss and a day’s worth of battle exertion tended towards stillness. He was standing at the map table, one arm held carefully at his side, reviewing something with Lü Yue, who stood opposite him looking like a man who had calculated the exact likelihood of suggesting his commander sit down and found it insufficient to make the attempt.

She took in the wound from across the tent. Field binding on the left upper arm — rough linen wrapped tight, dried blood in a pattern that told her the initial bleed had been significant but had slowed as expected. The arm moved when he gestured at the map, which told her the muscle function was intact and the bone almost certainly unaffected. Good. That simplified things considerably. He looked up when she entered. His gaze moved to her medical bag, then to her face, then back to the map with the swift efficiency of a man assessing a situation and incorporating new information without interrupting the previous one.

“Chief Physician Yun is occupied with serious cases. He sends me in his place. The wound is an arrow injury to the upper arm — I’ve treated two of the same type today. I have everything needed. With your permission, General,” she said, before he could ask.

A pause. Then: “Very well.”

She organised her supplies on the nearest flat surface — the salt-water solution, clean cloths, the stitching materials, the cleansing salve, fresh linen for the final dressing. She looked at the field binding. She would need to access the wound, which meant the sleeve, which meant asking him to —

She picked up the shears. “I’ll need to cut the sleeve. To access the wound without disturbing the binding until I’m ready to remove it properly,” she said.

He looked at the shears. He looked at her. Then, without speaking, he reached up and began unfastening his tunic. She hadn’t anticipated this. She had been prepared to cut the sleeve — a perfectly reasonable clinical approach that would have kept everything simple and contained. She hadn’t prepared herself for him to simply remove the whole garment in the efficient, matter-of-fact way of someone for whom physical exposure was purely practical.

The tunic came off. The undershirt followed. He placed them on the map table and turned back to her. Shiyu kept her eyes on the wound. She kept them there through an effort of will she suspected was visible and could do nothing about. The wound was there, in his upper left arm, and the wound was what she was here for, and she was going to look at the wound and the surrounding tissue and absolutely nothing else.

She was a physician. This was a patient. She could manage this. The wound was clean. The arrow had passed through the outer edge of the muscle without hitting anything critical. The field binding had been well-applied — someone in his guard knew what they were doing — and the bleed had largely stopped. She would need to clean it thoroughly, remove debris from the field dressing, close the wound in two layers, apply proper dressing with cleansing salve.

She opened the salt-water solution and began. The irrigation produced a brief, sharp intake of breath from him, controlled almost immediately. His jaw tightened for a moment and then resolved. She worked methodically, ensuring the wound bed was as clean as she could make it.

“This solution. I have seen it in your reports. The salt preparation,” he said, when the first stage was complete and she was preparing the stitching materials.

“Yes. Salt makes it hard for wound rot to take hold. The two together reduce wound complications significantly.”

“By what measure?”

“Compared to standard herbal compress treatment, wounds I have managed this way fester far less often. I’ve been tracking this in my reports.”

“I know. I have read them,” he said.

She placed the first stitch. Her hands were steady. Her heartbeat wasn’t, but her hands were steady and that was what mattered. He was quiet while she worked, the practised stillness of someone who had been through enough wound care to know that movement complicated things. She was placing the seventh stitch when he said, without particular emphasis, “Your heartbeat.”

She placed the eighth stitch.

“I can feel it through your hands. When you’re working close to the wound. It has been elevated since you entered the tent,” he said, still in that even tone.

The observation landed precisely where it was aimed, which was the truth. Her cheeks were warm. She was certain of this without needing to touch them.

“It has been a demanding day. The volume of cases. The sustained —” she said, carefully.

“You were entirely composed treating patients in the medical tent. Your uncle described your conduct as calm and effective throughout,” he said.

She tied off the eighth stitch.

He was quiet for a moment. “So it is something specific to this tent.”

She began the ninth stitch. She could feel him watching the side of her face. Not intrusively — he hadn’t moved, not changed the quality of his stillness. Simply watching. The way he watched everything: with complete, patient attention.

“Yes, it is something specific to this tent,” she said, after a pause that went slightly longer than she intended. The word came out low. Plainly. Without the careful framing she would have preferred to build around it, but she had used up her available misdirections.

She placed the final stitch. Tied it off. Checked the alignment of the closure — even tension, clean edges, good approximation. Her best work of the day, actually. One of the cleanest closures she had done in either of her lives. In the moment of sitting back slightly to examine the closure from distance, she was aware of how close she had been to him — the proximity that wound treatment required — and how she was now at a small remove, and at that remove she could see, peripherally, his face.

His expression was neutral. But a different neutral from his command tent, his formal settings. Quieter. Something underneath the neutrality that she couldn’t name but felt with a certainty she wasn’t going to examine.

She said, “The closure is complete. The wound is clean. No weight-bearing on the arm tonight, no combat use for at least five days. The stitches will need removal in ten days.”

“You,” he said.

She looked up from the wound.

“You placed the stitches. You should be the one to remove them. Continuity of care. It makes sense,” he said, in the tone of someone offering a straightforward practical reason.

It did make sense. It was perfectly reasonable. It was also the first thing he had said to her that wasn’t a directive or a clinical question, and she held it carefully in both hands.

“Ten days. I’ll come in the morning. Early,” she said.

“The hour of the Rabbit. Before the morning drum. Come then,” he said.

She finished the dressing, gathered her supplies, and left. Outside the tent she stopped and pressed the flat of her hand against the cool canvas for three heartbeats. Then she straightened, adjusted her bag, and went back to the medical tent.

Behind her, she heard Lü Yue’s voice, very quiet: “Is it just me, or did the General not take his eyes off her the entire time?”

She walked faster.

chapters.title: The Hour of the Rabbit
chapters.desc: He tells her to come at dawn to take the stitches out. She is early.
chapters.epigraph: “I revised the estimate based on observed progression. Seven will be sufficient.” — on the stitches, at the hour of the rabbit
chapters.content:
The camp at the hour of the Rabbit had a quality she had learned over her weeks there: the half-light between night watch and full activity, fires being stoked for the morning meal, the dusty-dry scent of the northern frontier that she now associated with the whole of her time here. She reached the command tent precisely at six, for the fourth morning in a row. He was at the map table, as he always was at this hour. Strong tea in a plain ceramic cup at his right hand, half-finished. Maps before him with notations in his hand — sparse, precise, directional. He looked up when she entered, set down what he was reading, and stood with the even movement of a man for whom the transition between tasks was simply a matter of completing one and beginning the next.

She directed him to the chair. She had learned this mattered in a medical context — not because he was difficult, but because the examination required a position and it was cleaner to state it than to hope he would choose correctly on his own. He sat. She organised her tools and began.

“The recovery analysis document. You added a proposed modification to the winter ration schedule,” he said, midway through the stitch removal.

“Yes.” She drew out the fourth stitch with the careful outward rotation that minimised tissue drag.

“The salt and dried protein adjustment. You argued it would reduce cold-weather wound complication rates.”

“The records from the autumn and winter recovery cases supported it. The difference in recovery rates between the heavily rationed units and the standard units was consistent across three seasons of records.”

“Wei Tiecheng objects on supply grounds.”

“I know. I read his annotation. His concern is logistical — the supply contract can’t absorb the change mid-season. He’s correct about that. The recommendation should be implemented at the start of the next supply cycle, not immediately.”

A pause.

“You read the command review annotations.”

A fractional hesitation. “My uncle’s copies. He reviews them as part of running the medical service. I read over his shoulder when the annotations were relevant to cases I had been treating.”

This wasn’t entirely the whole truth. She continued to the sixth stitch without looking at his face.

“Lü Yue asked me directly how you decided which results could be trusted. I told him to address the question to you,” the General said.

She stopped. One full breath. Then she continued working. “I would be glad to answer his question, if an opportunity presents itself.”

“It will. He reads the medical reports more carefully than anyone except me. He has an interest in the method.”

She freed the final stitch and stepped back to assess the healed closure — even scar formation, clean tissue, full integrity. Better than average for this wound type at this stage.

She said, “It has healed well. Full range of motion should be restored within another week. I would suggest avoiding anything that strains the arm against resistance for seven more days, but the structural healing is complete.”

“You said ten days initially.”

“I revised the estimate based on observed progression. Seven will be sufficient.”

She finished the light final wrap. He didn’t move from the chair — usually he stood the moment she declared a treatment complete, the body returning to its default readiness. He remained seated, watching her pack her bag with the steady attention she had never, in three weeks, successfully become immune to.

“Yun Shiyu,” he said.

She looked up, because not looking up would have been a form of avoidance she wasn’t going to allow herself.

“Your uncle and I have discussed the camp’s medical record-keeping. Some of your analysis work from the past three weeks will be incorporated into the formal system. Your way of tracking wound fever in particular. He believes it should be established as a standard practice.”

She waited.

“I have agreed to this. The method you developed will be attributed to you by name in the camp records. The Chief Physician has been instructed to implement it across all wound care documentation.”

Her hands stilled on the bag’s fastening.

“The attribution to me by name. If those records are ever reviewed by the provincial administration —” she said carefully.

“Your name is already in the camp’s records as a physician’s assistant who served during the eastern campaign recovery period. The attribution adds to that record. It does not create a new one.”

He was giving her professional legacy. In documents that would outlast her time in the camp, perhaps outlast her memory of this period — her name, attached to work she had done, making it permanent. She looked down at the fastening of her bag and spent three full heartbeats ensuring her breathing was even.

“Thank you, General,” she said. Her voice came out steady and she was grateful for it.

He stood. She moved towards the exit. At the flap she paused — not because she had planned to, but because something needed to be said. She turned back. He was at the map table, dispatch in hand.

“The work has been — I am glad I came here. Regardless of the manner of my coming, which I know was improper. The work has been worth doing. I am glad to have done it.” She stopped. Started again.

He didn’t look up immediately. When he did, his expression was the quiet unreadable one — complex, real, and not for her to claim.

“It has been worth having done,” he said. Which was a different thing from what she had said, and which she understood he had said deliberately.

She went back to the medical tent. Her uncle was at the preparation table. He looked at her once — the diagnostic look, quick and complete — and returned to his work without comment. She put away her bag, washed her hands, picked up the morning’s first case record. She was smiling. She was aware of this and didn’t attempt to suppress it, because her uncle had already seen it and pretending would only have been insulting to his intelligence.

She was also, beneath the warmth of the morning, beginning to understand that ten days had given her something she hadn’t anticipated when she had lain on her sleeping mat counting them: not resolution, not certainty, not the beginning of anything that could be named and claimed. But a genuine thing. A real exchange. Work recognised, words given and received, a small and careful expansion of the space between two people who had started with only her one-sided confession and his efficient management of a problem she represented.

It was better than what she had come here imagining — in the way that real things were better than imagined ones: harder to hold, less perfectly shaped, and entirely, unmistakably present.

chapters.title: The Last Week
chapters.desc: Her last days at the camp, and the men who finally say what they think of her.
chapters.epigraph: “Your time here has been of value to the camp. I wanted you to know I have noted it.” — the General
chapters.content:
The four remaining weeks of her original six passed with the momentum of time running towards an end that everyone can see but no one addresses directly. The camp continued its work. She continued hers. The post-battle recovery phase wound down and the daily patient volume returned to something close to the pre-battle baseline — the chronic conditions, the training injuries, the ordinary medical maintenance of a large body of men under field conditions. She treated them with the same thoroughness she had brought to the acute cases. Without entirely deciding to, she had begun to think of these men as her patients — not the Chief Physician’s patients she was helping to manage, but her own responsibility.

Lü Yue came to the medical tent in the third day of the final week — not for treatment but with a question. He arrived with the bearing of a man who considered even a visit to a tent worth conducting with appropriate gravity, and he asked her, in his measured and serious way, to explain how she had decided which of her recovery results could be trusted. She explained it. He listened with the complete attention of someone for whom understanding a thing properly mattered more than understanding it quickly. He asked two follow-up questions. She answered both.

When she finished, he was quiet for a moment. Then: “The logic is sound.”

Coming from Lü Yue, this wasn’t a small thing. Wei Tiecheng appeared the following day — standing in the entrance with his arms crossed, his face wearing the expression she had come to recognise as a man preparing to say something he had decided to say but wasn’t entirely comfortable saying.

He said, “The salt-water preparation. You treated twelve men from my unit in the acute phase. None of them festered. Two had wounds I’ve seen kill men in previous campaigns through contamination alone. You managed both cleanly.”

“The preparation was critical in those cases,” she said.

“Yes. Your time here has been of value to the camp. I wanted you to know I have noted it.” He uncrossed his arms.

It was the longest personal speech she had heard from him, and the cost of it had been visible in the careful construction.

“Thank you. That means a great deal,” she said.

The evening before her departure she wrote her final report. It was long — the complete post-battle recovery period, fully documented — and at the end she added a section she hadn’t been asked to write: a summary of her wound-cleaning method with detailed instructions for replication by any future physician who would use the camp’s records. She wrote it as clearly as she was capable of, in language accessible to someone who hadn’t developed the approach from the beginning. The point wasn’t that she had developed it but that it worked and should be used.

She sealed it and placed it at the top of the collection stack.

Then she began packing her bundle for the morning.

chapters.title: The Road South
chapters.desc: She rides home without looking back. Almost.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m still deciding whether to be angry with you. Come inside. Cook made the congee you like.” — Lady Ren
chapters.content:
The morning of her departure arrived with the clean, cold light of the northern frontier in the late season — the sky a flat pale blue, the air dry and clear. She had said her goodbyes to the patients the evening before, the natural concluding conversations of a physician completing her care. Gao, the soldier whose forearm she had stitched in her first week, had taken her hand in both of his and held on, which wasn’t done, and she had let him.

Her uncle walked with her to the southern exit. They didn’t speak much. The relationship between them had, over six weeks, arrived somewhere more honest and more complex than either of them had articulated. He had watched her work and had been proud, she understood — in the way that people who invest in someone and are proven right by that investment were permitted to feel. He had also worried. Both things were visible in his face.

At the exit he stopped. “Write to your mother. When you return to Qingzhou — and I mean this seriously, Shiyu — do not let what you have built here go to waste sitting in your father’s study. You have a physician’s mind and hands. Use them.”

“I intend to.”

“There will be proposals. From families who have heard of the governor’s daughter with unusual medical training. Your mother will bring them to you,” he said, his voice shifting to a gentler register.

She looked at the road south, which was already visible through the exit gate. She knew what she had done. She knew what she had found. She knew what she was leaving.

“I know,” she said.

He put his hand on her shoulder briefly — the same gesture from the day she had arrived, frightened and mortified and determined not to show either — and released her.

“Travel safely. I’m still deciding whether to be angry with you,” he said.

She smiled. He gave her the small nod that was his version of a smile in return. She turned and walked towards the escort. She didn’t look back at the medical tent. She did look, once, as the escort cleared the camp’s perimeter and the track turned east before south — she looked back at the camp as a whole, and found, or didn’t find, among the movement, the figure she was looking for.

He wasn’t visible. The command area was there — she could identify the tent from here — but there was no figure at the entrance, no one standing at the perimeter watching the departure. Of course there wasn’t. A general didn’t stand at the edges of his camp watching a physician’s assistant leave. He had a morning briefing. He had an empire to manage. She understood this. She had always understood it.

She turned her face south and rode.

On the second evening of the journey, she wrote in her personal notes for the first time since leaving Qingzhou. She wrote about the patients and the work, about Gao and his proprietary relationship with his own stitching, about Lü Yue’s careful questions and Wei Tiecheng and the cost of his acknowledgment. About Chen Ye’s habit of saying one true thing on his way out a door. About her uncle’s face when she had done something well.

She wrote one line about the General. Not the confession and not the battle and not the stitches or the heartbeat observed through her hands. Just one line:

It was worth having done.

She closed the notebook. She was, she found, neither happy nor unhappy in any simple sense. She was full — of experience, of work, of things that had mattered while they were happening and would continue to matter in the form of what she carried from them. She arrived in Qingzhou on the third afternoon. Her mother met her at the gate, crying in the contained way of a woman who had been worrying for six weeks and had run out of the energy to manage it with full composure.

“I am well, Mother,” Shiyu said, into the fabric of her mother’s shoulder.

“I know you’re well. I was still worried.”

Her father appeared in the courtyard with the expression of a man experiencing several emotions simultaneously and resolving this by being very calm about all of them. He had ink on his sleeve, as always. He looked at his daughter over his wife’s shoulder and gave her the small fond nod of a man who was relieved and also still somewhat bewildered by the child he had been given, which was the same way he had been looking at her for sixteen years.

“You’re back,” he said.

“I’m back.”

“Good. Come inside. Cook made the congee you like.”

She went inside, and ate, and was home. She slept twelve hours that first night, which she hadn’t done since she was five years old and the soul she carried had first, bewilderingly, opened its eyes in this body. She woke to the familiar smell of the governor’s residence and lay still for a moment, looking at the ceiling she had looked at her whole life in this world, and felt the six weeks settle into the past where they belonged.

She was home. She had work to do. She got up.

chapters.title: Three Years
chapters.desc: A clinic of her own, a nickname she finds excessive, and a life built on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “The clinic will need a proper sign. Something that looks established.” — Yun Shiyu, seventeen, very sure
chapters.content:
The clinic took eight months to establish from the day she first raised it with her father to the day she saw her first patient through its door. Eight months of persuasion, conducted with the systematic patience she now applied to all long campaigns — building the case piece by piece, addressing each concern her father raised before he could raise it again, demonstrating that the plan was sound and the need was real and the person proposing it wasn’t simply a girl with an impractical idea but someone who had spent six weeks treating battle casualties and three months before that building a foundation of medical knowledge that most trained physicians in Qingzhou couldn’t match.

Her father eventually said yes in the way he said yes to her important requests — not with immediate enthusiasm but with the gradual, thoughtful agreement of a man who had examined all available arguments and found none sufficient to outweigh her. Her mother’s response was more complicated. Lady Ren was a woman of profound conventional instincts who loved her daughter with a thoroughness that included wanting her to have a life that resembled the lives of people she understood. A daughter who opened a medical clinic at sixteen — seventeen by the time it opened — and worked in it herself as the primary physician, treating patients from all levels of the city’s society, wasn’t that life.

But Lady Ren was also a woman who had watched her daughter for sixteen years and had never, not once, been able to make her into something she wasn’t. She had made her peace with this. Not easily, but genuinely.

“The clinic will need a proper sign. Something that looks established. We’ll ask the best woodworker in the eastern district,” she had said, on the day she agreed not to object further.

Qingyun Yiguan — the Qingcloud Medical Hall. The characters carved by the best woodworker in Qingzhou, painted in the colour she had chosen, hung on the day she stood beneath it and felt something settle. The first year was the hardest in the way that first years of built things were hardest: the proving of the concept against the resistance of an environment that hadn’t yet decided what it thought of her. She was the governor’s daughter, which opened some doors and closed others — the city’s conventional families preferred their physicians to be older men, trained under established masters, without the irregular history of a girl who had apparently spent six weeks in a military camp. She treated whoever came, with whoever came. She was, and persistently, excellent.

The second year was different. The river worker with the crush injury that two other physicians had suggested amputating — she spent two months on him and he walked out carrying his own weight. The fever cluster in the eastern district that she traced to a contaminated well before the outbreak spread. The woman who came to her as a last resort after three years of a condition that had been treated with everything available and hadn’t improved, and who Shiyu diagnosed correctly in the first consultation by asking questions no one had thought to ask.

Word travelled. Not loudly, not officially, but in the way of cities where people talked to each other — the kind of talk that followed results rather than reputation.

By the third year they called her the Fairy Physician, which she found slightly excessive. She was simply thorough, and honest about what she knew and didn’t know, and she took her work seriously. These weren’t supernatural qualities. She built a life. She built it deliberately, with the same care she brought to her medicine, and it was substantially hers. She also, in the quiet of the prep room in the early mornings before the clinic opened, kept her uncle’s letters in a dedicated correspondence box and read them carefully from beginning to end, including the sections about the camp’s medical service and the sections about Lü Yue’s questions and the sections about the documentation system’s expansion.

She didn’t read them for information about the General. She read them for information about the camp’s medical service, about her uncle’s work, about the camp she had known for six weeks and which had given her the foundation for everything she had built since. This was entirely true. It was also not the entire truth, and she was honest with herself about this in the privacy of her own mind, which was the one place she didn’t require herself to perform.

She had built something real. She wasn’t waiting. She was building, and the building was the thing, and whatever she felt — and it was still there, persistent and unresolved, the way certain things simply were — lived alongside the building rather than instead of it. She wasn’t sixteen anymore. She was nineteen, and she was the Fairy Physician of Qingzhou, and her clinic had three years of records that were the most rigorous civilian medical documentation in the province.

This was enough. She had made it enough. She had also, she was honest enough to admit, made it very good — in case anyone was ever in a position to see it.

chapters.title: Mei Yun
chapters.desc: A fifteen-year-old talks her way into the clinic and notices far too much.
chapters.epigraph: “You receive a letter from your uncle every two weeks.” “He writes regularly.” “I’m just observing.” — Mei Yun, fifteen
chapters.content:
Mei Yun appeared at the clinic on the morning of the second year’s fourth month, carrying a note from her mother and the expression of a girl who had decided something and wasn’t going to be talked out of it. She was fifteen, with the slight build and sharp eyes of someone who had been paying close attention to the world for longer than most people her age. She had heard about the Fairy Physician, she said. She wanted to learn medicine. She was willing to do whatever the clinic required — cleaning, preparation work, assisting with patients, anything. She had good hands, she added, holding them out as evidence, and she did — capable, steady, the hands of someone with fine motor control and patience.

Shiyu hired her on the spot. Not out of charity — the clinic needed a second pair of hands — but because the girl’s directness reminded her of something. The quality of someone who had decided what mattered and was simply pursuing it, without the elaborate social performance that usually surrounded requests of this kind. Mei Yun was, it turned out, perceptive to a degree that occasionally bordered on inconvenient.

She had excellent hands and a genuine aptitude for the massage and circulation work that was rapidly becoming one of the clinic’s most valued specialties. She had good bedside manner — a quality that couldn’t be taught entirely, only cultivated in someone who already had the instinct for it, and she had it. She learned quickly, asked real questions, and made the reasonable mistakes of someone paying close enough attention to know where the edges were.

She also narrated the world to herself as though she were reading it from a story, which she occasionally did out loud at moments that weren’t entirely convenient.

“You receive a letter from your uncle every two weeks,” she observed, approximately three months after joining the clinic, while she was laying out the morning’s treatment materials.

“He writes regularly,” Shiyu said.

“The ones on the two-week cycle are different from the monthly ones. You read the monthly ones at the documentation table. You read the two-week ones at the window.”

Shiyu set down the preparation she had been holding. “Mei Yun.”

“I’m just observing,” she said serenely, and went back to the treatment materials.

The two-week letters from her uncle had, in fact, begun to include a kind of paragraph that arrived at the end, set apart from the professional content. Observations about the camp. A note about how the documentation system was performing. A mention of the wound-cleaning method and how it had been applied. Nothing direct. Nothing that required her to respond to anything in particular. But present. Consistent. Arriving every two weeks without exception, on the cycle that matched the northern dispatch schedule.

She read them at the window because the light was better there. This was the reason. It was the only reason she had.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.desc: The northern army comes through Qingzhou with a wounded officer, and asks for the Fairy Physician.
chapters.epigraph: “She’s the Fairy Physician.” — Mei Yun, helpfully, from behind Shiyu’s left shoulder
chapters.content:
Her father appeared in the clinic doorway on an ordinary afternoon in early autumn, and the his expression — fond, slightly bewildered, carrying information he wasn’t sure how to deliver — told her the day was about to become something other than ordinary.

He said, “There is a military procession passing through Qingzhou. The northern army, returning from a campaign. The General is among them. One of his officers has an arrow wound in the leg that requires treatment. The garrison captain came to us. He asked specifically for the Fairy Physician.” He paused, with the delicacy of a man navigating something he could see but not quite map.

Shiyu was quiet for a moment. She thought, with the clarity of someone who had spent three years becoming a physician of genuine standing: the patient has a wound that requires treatment. She thought, with the honesty she kept reserved for herself: he is in my city. She thought, with the pragmatism of someone who had built something real and wasn’t going to betray it with either panic or performance: I am the physician the garrison captain asked for, and I am going to that inn and I am going to treat the wound.

She folded her apron. She picked up her medical bag. She told Mei Yun to bring the supply case and the massage materials.

“We’re going to the Jade Phoenix Inn,” she said.

Mei Yun looked at her with the sharp, quiet eyes she brought to everything. “Of course,” she said, in the tone of someone for whom the situation was exactly as significant as it appeared, and who was going to comport herself accordingly.

They walked. The Jade Phoenix occupied the best address on Qingzhou’s central avenue — dark timber and pale plaster, three stories, the kind of understated quality that communicated expense without announcing it. The stable yard was clean. The innkeeper had the slightly overwhelmed bearing of a man whose establishment had been occupied by a general’s retinue for the past four hours and was managing it with professional competence at some personal cost.

She adjusted the strap of her medical bag. She exhaled once through her nose.

Then she went in. The private suite at the inn’s eastern end. The room had been prepared correctly — she noticed this before she noticed anything else, the systematic thinking that had organised the space for treatment rather than comfort: the bed shifted to a treatment-accessible position, the surface nearest the window cleared for medical work, additional lamps brought in for adequate light. Someone in his retinue had thought about this. Someone in his retinue always thought about this.

Zhou Hua was on the bed, his right leg elevated on folded blankets, his face wearing the expression of a man in moderate pain who was pretending otherwise. He was thirty-two, lean and wiry, his sun-darkened skin a shade paler than she would have liked to see. The field dressing on his leg showed the dried evidence of a wound that had bled significantly before being controlled. Around him stood four of the five officers she remembered.

Wei Tiecheng near the window, arms crossed, thirty-eight and no less substantial than three years ago, the scar on his left cheek still its exact same colour. Lin Wenyuan in the single chair with a document that hadn’t been consulted in some time given the angle at which he was holding it. Lü Yue at the bedside with the gravity of a man standing watch over something important. Chen Ye at the far wall, and he was the one whose expression changed first — the very slight shift she recognised as surprise controlled into a more socially acceptable form.

And in the room’s far corner, standing at the window with his back to her —she didn’t look at him. Not yet. She crossed directly to the bed.

“Commander Zhōu. I’m the physician from the Qingcloud Medical Hall. I’ll need to examine the wound. Can you describe the circumstances of the injury?”

Zhou Hua looked at her with the uncertain recognition of someone whose memory was working towards a conclusion it hadn’t quite reached yet.

“She’s the Fairy Physician,” Mei Yun said helpfully, from behind Shiyu’s left shoulder, using the name the city had given her in the tone of someone presenting a professional credential.

Wei Tiecheng’s head turned from the window. Lin Wenyuan set down his document. Lü Yue looked at her with the careful attention of a man confirming something. And Chen Ye said, with the lightness she recognised as something other than casualness, “The Qingcloud Medical Hall. Eastern district of Qingzhou. Established approximately three years ago… Yun Shiyu.” The name came last, like someone placing the final piece.

Her name in the room. She didn’t turn towards the window. She didn’t look at the corner where the General stood. She looked at Zhou Hua and kept her hands moving with the purposeful preparation of a physician getting to work.

“The arrow wound. When it happened — what was the trajectory?” she said.

Zhou Hua blinked. Then, with the adaptability of a soldier who had spent years following rapid changes in situation, he began to describe the incident. Behind her, from the window corner, she heard nothing. No words. No movement. Only the quality of a presence she had learned, three years ago, to recognise the way one recognised weather — not always visible, but always felt. She began the examination. Her hands were steady.

She was a physician. This was her work. She didn’t look towards the window for the first quarter of an hour. Then, reaching for a fresh instrument, she moved slightly — and found that he had shifted from the window corner. He was at the room’s perimeter, closer to the bed. Not intrusively close. Simply present, at the distance of a man who had chosen to watch rather than to stand apart.

He was watching her hands. Not her face. Her hands. The way he had watched them in the command tent three years ago, with the focused attention of someone absorbing technique. She looked away. She opened her supply case. She did her work.

chapters.title: The Five Days
chapters.desc: She treats Zhou Hua’s leg and does not look at the window. For a while.
chapters.epigraph: “You remind me of someone. A physician’s assistant we had, three years ago.” — Commander Zhou Hua, from the bed
chapters.content:
The wound was serious but manageable. Arrow into the outer thigh at an angle, passing through the muscle without striking the bone. Field dressing had done its job — bleeding controlled, wound not yet significantly contaminated. She would need to clean it thoroughly, close it in two layers, apply proper dressing with cleansing salve. A straightforward procedure, in any other room. She cleaned the wound with the thorough precision its contamination risk warranted. She talked Zhou Hua through the deeper stitching layer — warning him before each significant moment, keeping her voice at the level that said the situation was controlled and he need not worry about it, which was the register she used for patients who were more frightened than they were willing to admit.

“You’re good at that. The talking. Telling me what’s coming before it comes,” Zhou Hua said, watching the ceiling.

“If you know what’s next, your body doesn’t brace for the unknown version of it, which is always worse than the actual version.”

“Hm. You remind me of someone. A physician’s assistant we had, three years ago. After the eastern engagement. Except she was younger. I think.” He seemed to be working his way towards a thought.

“The salt-water solution. That’s the same preparation,” Lin Wenyuan said, from somewhere behind her, with the precision of someone who had been reading a document for the past quarter of an hour and hadn’t, in fact, been reading it.

She placed the next stitch.

“It is her. I told you when she walked in,” Chen Ye said, simply.

From the room’s perimeter, the General said nothing. Shiyu worked through the external layer of the closure with the patient precision of someone for whom the quality of the work wasn’t something that could be sacrificed to the complexity of the surrounding circumstances. Each stitch was placed correctly. The tension was even. The wound edges came together cleanly. She finished. She applied the cleansing salve and began the final dressing.

“Mei Yun, begin the preliminary circulation assessment on the foot and lower calf,” she said.

Mei Yun moved into position, her hands already warm from preparation, and began.

Zhou Hua made a sound of involuntary surprise. “That is — that’s quite strong.”

“Your circulation has been partially restricted by the wound’s position. The massage will prevent stiffness and reduce the risk of complications from reduced blood flow. It will be uncomfortable initially.”

“Is uncomfortable the word you’re looking for?”

“It’s accurate,” she said.

From the direction of the window, she heard something — a brief, very quiet sound from the General. Not words. Just the almost-nothing of someone suppressing a reaction. The sound that, if she was reading it correctly — and she believed she was — was close to amusement. She didn’t look up from her notes. But she felt, in the same way she felt his position in the room without looking at it, that the sound had been something warm.
