The corner of his mouth. The thing that wasn’t quite a smile and was, she had decided, one of the most significant expressions she had ever seen on a human face.

“Tonight,” he said.

“Tonight,” she said.

She went through to the waiting room.

“Old Master Feng. The knee?” she said.

“Better every week. For the physician. And for whoever else you have in the consultation room, because I heard two voices in there and the other one is not Mei Yun,” he said, with the satisfaction of a man who was healing correctly and knew it. He held up the loquats.

Mei Yun, in the corner, was very carefully arranging the morning’s supply trays in a way that required complete visual attention.

“Thank you, Master Feng. Let’s look at that knee,” Shiyu said.

She treated the knee. She treated the four patients after him. She did her work with the thoroughness she had always brought to it, the same care that had made Old Master Feng whole and the river worker whole and the clinic real.

At midday she came through to the preparation room and found him there — not in the consultation room but in the preparation room, having apparently been shown the herb cabinet by Mei Yun, who had apparently decided that the General’s visit to the clinic should include a full orientation. He was reading the label on a jar of dried mugwort with the focused attention he gave everything.

“Mei Yun gave you a tour,” she said.

“She was thorough.”

“She is always thorough.”

He set down the jar. He looked at her across the preparation room, in the midday light through the eastern window, with the herb cabinet behind him and three years of her work on the shelves around them, and his expression was the one she had no words for — the one without the containment, just him, looking.

“The work is —” he began.

“Don’t. You don’t have to find the words for it. I know,” she said gently.

He was quiet for a moment. “Yes, you do,” he said.

She crossed to the preparation table and began the midday compound work, because there were afternoon patients and the work didn’t stop and she had always found that the work was a good thing to do with feelings that were too large for standing still. After a moment he pulled the second stool from the wall and sat beside her. He didn’t help — she hadn’t asked him and the compound work was precise and required her specific knowledge. He simply sat. Present. In the way he was present in rooms: paying attention to everything, performing nothing.

She worked. He sat. Outside, Qingzhou moved through its midday in the way it always did — the river district sounds, the herb market smell, the a city where things grew rather than converged. She thought about a balcony and a girl who had pressed her hand to her cheek and said: purely academic. She thought about a supply compartment and four hours of reconsidering. She thought about a tent and a confession and three heartbeats of an unguarded expression. She thought about the southern well and the reports written by lamplight and a heartbeat felt through stitching hands and one word spoken flat and certain in a quiet room in the capital.

She thought: this is what it looks like, finally, on the other side of all of that. It looked like this: a preparation room in Qingzhou in the midday light, with herb jars on the shelves and a mortar in her hands and the General of the northern army on a stool beside her, not speaking, simply there. It was, she decided, exactly right.

chapters.title: The Dinner Her Mother Had Planned for Months
chapters.desc: He comes to dinner with a gift for her father, and her mother asks if he eats alone.
chapters.epigraph: “You have no family in the capital? No household to return to in the evenings?” — Lady Ren, who had planned this for months
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
Her mother had been preparing for this dinner since the capital. Shiyu understood this when she saw the table. The good lacquerware. The arrangement of the dishes — the ones her grandmother had favoured, the ones that said: this household isn’t performing, it has standards that precede this occasion. The chrysanthemum tea prepared at the correct temperature and not a degree warmer. The courtyard lanterns lit at the proper angle to cast the best light on the south-facing gate.

Her mother had made no fuss about any of this. She had simply done it, in the quiet and absolute way she did everything that mattered to her, and the result was a table that said: you are welcome here, without saying it, which was the only way it counted. The General arrived precisely when he said he would. This was, she had come to understand, a structural feature of who he was — not punctuality as performance but punctuality as respect, the acknowledgment that other people’s time had value. He came with Chen Ye, who was there in the capacity of — it was never quite specified, but Chen Ye always seemed to find a role in rooms where he arrived.

Her father met them at the gate. She watched from inside the courtyard doorway, because going to the gate herself would have been correct etiquette and she was, in this moment, not entirely in command of her own face. Her father bowed to the General in the way he had developed for people he wasn’t quite sure how to address — the warm, slightly flustered bow of a man who was a governor and a scholar and had spent fifty-five years being exactly what he was and had never once had occasion to greet a supreme military commander as a dinner guest.

The General returned the bow with the stillness she associated with him receiving unexpected things — not uncomfortable, simply absorbing. Then he produced the gift his household had prepared: a set of herbal classification texts, the Tang dynasty edition, the companion volumes to the ones her father had accessed at the Imperial Medical Library. He presented them with two hands and the correct phrase of courtesy. Her father looked at the texts.

Then he looked at the General.

Then he said, in the slightly undone voice of a man encountering something that had required thought: “You found the companion volumes.”

“I was told there was a gap in the set,” the General said.

Her father held the texts with the careful reverence of someone handling something long sought. He didn’t say anything else for a moment. He didn’t need to. Shiyu stepped into the courtyard. The General saw her the moment she moved — she had noticed this about him, that his attention tracked movement in a room the way a strategist tracked position on a map, not threatening but complete. His gaze moved to her and stayed, in the way it had been staying since the clinic that morning, and she thought: he has been inside my clinic for half a day, in the city I built, and nothing about his expression has said anything other than that he is exactly where he chose to be.

She gave him the correct greeting for the occasion. He returned it. Chen Ye, entering behind him, caught her eye briefly with the air of a man who had been correct about something for three years and was experiencing quiet professional satisfaction. Dinner was excellent. This was true in the practical sense — the food was good, the preparation careful, the pacing considered — and also in the more particular sense that every person at the table was, for different reasons, exactly themselves.

Her father had recovered from the texts and was now in full intellectual form, which meant he was talking with sustained enthusiasm about the Tang dynasty’s way of classifying and its implications for current Qingzhou herb cultivation. The General listened to this — actually listened, not the attentive performance of a superior guest, but the engaged focus of someone who found the subject worth following. He asked two questions. Both were good. Her father’s delight at having good questions asked was visible and slightly undignified and entirely endearing.

Her mother served tea with the composed serenity of a woman for whom this dinner was proceeding exactly as she had known it would, which was itself a form of authority. Chen Ye, at the table’s far end, had fallen into conversation with Mei Yun — who had been invited on the grounds that she was the clinic’s assistant and practically household — and their exchange had the quality of two people who were both significantly sharper than the setting required and had recognised this in each other.

Shiyu ate her soup and was present and engaged and simultaneously aware, in the way she had been aware for three and a half years, that the person across the table from her had moved three seats closer than the formal arrangement would have placed him, and that her mother had arranged the seating.

At the second course, her mother asked the General, with the gentle precision of a woman who chose her moments: “You have no family in the capital? No household to return to in the evenings?”

A brief pause. The kind that, from him, communicated consideration rather than discomfort. “My household is managed by staff. My family — My parents passed when I was fifteen. The Emperor’s household served in that role afterward, as much as it could.” He paused again, and something in the pause was careful in a way that wasn’t evasion but honesty about something he didn’t reach for easily.

Her mother looked at him with the expression she wore when she was deciding something. “Then you eat alone in the evenings,” she said, and it wasn’t quite a question.

“When there is an evening,” he said, which was the exact kind of answer that told you everything about a person’s life.

Her mother refilled his tea without further comment. But she did it with the care she reserved for people she had decided to feed properly, and Shiyu saw this and set down her chopsticks for a moment and breathed. Her father produced his notebook at the dessert course to show the General the herb specimen notes from the capital road stop. This was possibly not the most conventional dinner-table offering, but the General accepted the notebook and looked at it with the same engaged attention he had given everything else, and her father’s face when someone took his notes seriously was the face of a man entirely happy.

It was the best dinner she could remember sitting at. Not because it was elaborate. Because everyone at it was real.

Afterward, in the courtyard, with the summer night closing in and the lanterns giving everything a warm and uncertain gold, she stood beside him for a moment while the others were occupied — her father drawing her uncle — who had ridden down from the camp with the review party — into the notebook discussion, Chen Ye and Mei Yun in animated argument about something near the gate, her mother visible through the interior window, composed and present and deliberately not watching.

“Your father is going to read those texts tonight,” the General said.

“He started before dessert was finished. I saw his hands.”

The corner of his mouth. That exact thing. She had been watching it happen over months and she still hadn’t become immune to it.

“The clinic was quiet this afternoon. The patients were all straightforward. I keep thinking something will be difficult, and then it isn’t,” she said.

“That is what good preparation looks like from the outside. Routine,” he said.

She turned to look at him. He was looking at the courtyard — the familiar view of her family’s garden, the dark tile roof against the summer sky — and his expression was the quiet one. Simpler than the command tent, simpler even than the capital. The expression of someone for whom this place, this evening, was something other than ordinary.

She thought: he has been to courts and campaigns and imperial audiences and the Emperor’s own table. He is standing in the garden of a provincial governor eating conversation about Tang dynasty herbs and he looks like a man exactly where he intends to be.

“I am glad you came. For the review. And for the other reasons,” she said.

He looked at her. Something moved in his expression — the thing without a name, the one she had no words for — and then he said, simply: “So am I.”

She was very careful about her face. She succeeded, this time, only partially.

From the gate, Mei Yun’s voice, very quiet: “Chen Ye. Don’t look.”

Chen Ye’s voice: “I’m not looking.”

A pause.

“You’re looking.”

“I’m looking at the sky.”

He left at the correct hour — not early, which would have communicated he was managing something, and not late, which would have been a statement of its own. The correct hour, with the correct leave-taking, and when he said good night to her at the gate it was with the full attention he gave to things he considered worth attending to. She watched the gate close. Her mother appeared beside her.

They stood together for a moment in the quiet courtyard.

“He found the companion volumes,” her mother said.

“He did.”

“For your father. He asked someone, Shiyu. He found out what your father needed and he asked someone to find it and he brought it to dinner.”

“I know,” she said.

Her mother pressed her hand once, and went inside. Shiyu stood in the courtyard for another moment and let herself feel the full and specific warmth of it — the evening, the texts, the question about eating alone, the not-quite-smile — and then she went inside and made the next morning’s herbal preparations and was, when she was honest with herself, happier than she had been in a very long time.

chapters.title: Peng Yao
chapters.desc: A pleasant new secretary delivers papers in person and looks at the wrong cabinet.
chapters.epigraph: “He looked at your bookshelves. For longer than the left.” — Mei Yun, on the new secretary
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
She met Peng Yao on the second day of the General’s review visit. He arrived at the clinic mid-morning with the administrative documentation for the seasonal filing — a task that could have been sent through the garrison post, but which he delivered in person with a politeness so complete it was difficult to find any specific fault with it. He was thirty-one, she estimated. Scholar’s hands, well-kept, with the grooming of a man who had spent time in capital administrative circles. Intelligent face, pleasant features, the bearing of someone who had been in rooms with important people long enough to know how to move in them. He introduced himself with the correct degree of deference to her professional role and the correct degree of warmth to avoid seeming merely formal, and he had brought the documentation exactly right — organised, nothing missing, the kind of preparation that communicated competence.

She thanked him. She reviewed the filing. She raised two questions about the format for the seasonal baseline records. He answered both quickly, correctly. She found nothing specifically wrong with any of this. She also found herself paying attention in the way she paid attention to patients who presented with symptoms that didn’t quite resolve into a clear picture — the clinical attentiveness of a person who had learned to trust the thing that didn’t resolve.

Mei Yun was in the preparation room throughout. She said nothing. When Peng Yao left — correctly, pleasantly, with appropriate thanks — Mei Yun appeared in the consultation room doorway and looked at Shiyu with the expression of someone composing a sentence.

“He looked at your bookshelves,” Mei Yun said.

“Most visitors do.”

“He looked at the commission records cabinet.”

Shiyu looked up from the filing.

Mei Yun said, “The general commission documentation, is on the left side of the cabinet. The method records and the direct-channel correspondence are on the right. He looked specifically at the right side. For longer than the left.”

She was quiet for a moment. “Note it,” she said, and returned to the filing.

She noted it to her uncle that evening, through the commission channel, in the matter-of-fact language she used for observations she couldn’t yet categorize. Her uncle’s reply came the following morning. Brief. Peng Yao had been transferred to the civilian medical commission’s staff eight months ago. He came from the Ministry of Revenue’s capital administrative staff, recommended by a deputy minister whose name her uncle wrote without comment. He had no military background. He had submitted, in his first month, an internal review suggesting the commission’s method evaluation standards were insufficiently rigorous and that its chief civilian physician’s credentials should be formally verified by a capital academic board rather than accepted on the basis of field outcomes.

Her uncle had rejected this suggestion at the time. He hadn’t mentioned it to her. He wrote now, in the careful tone he used when something had proven more relevant than he expected: I believe I should have told you earlier. I thought it was bureaucratic friction. I am less certain of that now. She read this twice.

Then she filed it in the correspondence box, in the section she used for things she wasn’t going to act on immediately but wasn’t going to set aside. She went to see the General that afternoon, for the second day of the review. The work was good. The figures were useful. She raised, at the end of the session — with the neutral, clinical directness she had learned to trust as her most reliable instrument — what her uncle had written.

He listened without expression. He asked one question: the name of the deputy minister who had made the recommendation. She gave it. Something shifted in his face — barely, a degree, the tightening she associated with a man absorbing information that had connected with something he already knew. He didn’t share what it had connected with.

“I’ll look into it,” he said.

“I’m not asking you to act on it. I wanted you to know,” she said.

He looked at her. “I know. It is the same reason I tell you things,” he said.

She held this. The review continued. The figures were excellent. She presented the summer analysis with the focused engagement she always brought to work she found interesting, and he listened with the same focus, and for the hour that followed the world outside the consultation room was simply not the priority. It was only afterward, walking back through Qingzhou in the afternoon light, that she let herself think about the deputy minister’s name and the commission records on the right side of the cabinet. And she thought: Peng Yao came here himself. To this clinic, in person, with papers that could have been sent by post.

She thought about this carefully. And she filed it alongside what her uncle had written.

chapters.title: The Third Day
chapters.desc: The last day of the review, and he tells her what he sees in her work.
chapters.epigraph: “You have never once overestimated a clinical outcome in three years of records.” — the General, on the third day
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
The third day of the review was the last the General had scheduled in Qingzhou before returning north. She had known this. She had written it in her planning records with the same notation she gave every other date and had kept herself from annotating it. This was something she had been practising — not managing feelings into smaller things, but not allowing them to distort the shape of the days that held them. The day was what it was. She would be in it.

The morning session was productive in the way their work sessions had always been productive: engaged, honest, without the performance of two people who were only there for the work. The circulation treatment figures from the summer was strong — stronger than the first year’s projections, which had been conservative by design. He noted this. She explained the design choice in the same way she had explained it at the capital: underestimate and exceed rather than overestimate and disappoint.

“You have never once overestimated a clinical outcome in three years of records,” he said.

She looked up.

“Every projection in the baseline records is conservative. Every actual outcome exceeds it. The pattern is consistent enough to be a method rather than caution,” he said.

“I know what the work can do. I don’t always know what the patient’s circumstances will allow,” she said.

“You trust the work. You don’t trust the variables outside it,” he said.

She considered this for a moment. “That is probably accurate.”

“It makes for better records. It is also consistent with how you treat people,” he said, and the pause between the two was shorter than his pauses usually were.

She set down the season’s file. He was looking at the table — the familiar slight downward angle when he was being precise about something he had considered. And then he looked up at her, with the direct, steady quality she had been learning since the command tent, and he said, “The commission review. I will return in three months. The figures will be ready by then — the summer baseline comparison will be worth examining together.”

“Yes,” she said.

“I will come earlier. If that is acceptable.”

“Three months is a long time,” she said, which was honest and also the most she was prepared to say in the consultation room at midday with patients in an hour.

“It is,” he said. And from him, that was considerable.

She picked up the file. She returned to the figures. They worked through the remaining review items with the thoroughness both of them brought to things worth doing properly.

At the end, when the documentation was complete and she was gathering the clinic copies, she was aware of him not immediately standing. He sat for a moment at the table — not with the operational stillness of the command tent but the quieter stillness she had come to associate with him in the clinic. The stillness of someone present in a room rather than managing one.

“The shelves,” he said.

She looked up. He was looking at the herb cabinet — the one he had examined on the first day — and his expression was the one she had no words for.

“You built all of this. From nothing,” he said. Quietly. As a plain fact.

“From a plan and three years. And my father’s tolerance and my uncle’s records and a woodworker who did excellent work,” she said.

“From you,” he said. Looking at her. Not from nothing. From you.

She stood at the preparation table with a season’s file in her hands and the midday light through the eastern window and three and a half years of everything it had taken to arrive at this moment, and she thought: I have wanted, for a very long time, to be seen. Not as the physician’s useful resource, not as the governor’s unusual daughter, not as the girl in the supply compartment. As exactly what I am.

She thought: he sees it.

“Three months,” she said.

“Three months,” he said.

She didn’t watch him leave from the doorway. She went back to the preparation room and made the afternoon compound with steadiness in her hands, and she let herself feel what she felt without making it smaller, and the afternoon was warm and good and entirely real.

chapters.title: Peng Yao, Again
chapters.desc: Peng Yao keeps asking about the letters, and she asks the General not to manage around her.
chapters.epigraph: Yes. You are right. I will not manage around you again. — eleven words, morning light, the clinic window
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
The weeks after the General’s return north had the quality she had come to trust: the productive quiet of a life that was substantially hers. The clinic’s summer patient load followed the seasonal patterns she had documented for three years — river workers with sun exposure, farmers with repetitive stress injuries, the east district’s perennial dehydration problem that she had finally convinced three neighbourhood well-masters to address with covered wells and clean catchment.

The letters came on the two-week interval. She didn’t count the days between them. She noticed, accurately, when they arrived. Peng Yao came to the clinic twice more in that period. Both times with administrative documentation that was, technically, correctly timed for the commission cycle. Both times in person, with the smooth and pleasant manner she had learned to read beneath without finding easy purchase.

On the second visit, Mei Yun came to her afterward with the look of someone who had made an observation and had decided it warranted more than her usual sidelong delivery.

“He asked, whether the direct correspondence channel between the clinic and the command was a standard commission feature, or specific to this site,” Mei Yun said.

Shiyu set down her brush. “What did you tell him?”

“I told him I managed the supplies, not the administration, and that he should direct documentation questions through the garrison channel. He rephrased it twice.”

She looked at Mei Yun. Mei Yun looked back with the expression of someone who narrated the world as a story and had just identified the chapter they were in.

“He isn’t interested in our methods,” Shiyu said.

“No,” Mei Yun agreed.

She wrote to her uncle that evening. Not about Peng Yao’s questions — she would handle those through her own documentation, keep the record clean, give nothing that could be misread or extracted. She wrote about the commission figures, the summer baseline, the two legitimate method questions that had arisen from the summer analysis.

At the end, in the final paragraph, she wrote: I am being careful. I want you to know I am paying attention. Her uncle’s reply, two days later, was brief: I know you are. So is he. Be well. She filed it. She opened the clinic. She treated Old Master Feng’s knee and the river worker’s shoulder and the merchant woman’s recurring headaches that were, she had concluded after three careful assessments, caused by the blood vessels and entirely manageable with the herbal preparation she had refined over the year. She was a physician. She did her work. She let the work be what it was.

She also wrote to the General — through the direct channel, in the commission-framed language that was and wasn’t only the commission — and mentioned that the administrative documentation for the summer cycle had been arriving in person rather than through the garrison post. She mentioned it as a fact. She didn’t frame it as concern. He wrote back in five days, which was shorter than the usual two-week interval. He answered the commission questions first, all of them, correctly. At the end:

I am aware of Peng Yao. The deputy minister who recommended him has interests in the capital that conflict with the civilian commission’s expansion. I should have told you this when you first mentioned his name. I am telling you now. The situation is being monitored. If anything changes in how he approaches the clinic, write to me directly, the same day.

She read this three times. He had known. He had known from the day she gave him the deputy minister’s name, had known something she hadn’t known, and had made the calculation — the same calculation he made in military contexts, she understood, the one about what information to act on when and through which channel — and had chosen to tell her now rather than then. She wasn’t certain how she felt about this. She understood it — the logic was his logic, complete and sound. She also felt the friction of wanting to be in the situation rather than managed around it.

She wrote back:

Thank you for telling me. I would prefer, in future, to be in possession of relevant information at the time it becomes relevant. I understand your reasoning. I want you to understand mine.

She sealed it. She sent it. His reply came in three days:

Yes. You are right. I will not manage around you again.

Eleven words. She read them in the morning light at the clinic window.

She thought: he does not give ground easily. When he gives it, it is real.

She thought: this is what it means to know someone, actually. She went back to work.

chapters.title: The Storm
chapters.desc: A notice arrives to stop the letters. She writes to ask if he allowed it.
chapters.epigraph: “The complication is administrative.” “Administrative.” — Lady Ren, who had been reading situations her whole life
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
The storm arrived on the ninth day of the seventh month, which wasn’t unusual for Qingzhou in the summer season — the province was known for its rains, the architecture of the city designed across centuries for water management, the stone-paved streets angled towards the river district’s drainage. What was unusual was the letter that arrived that morning. It came through the garrison, official seal, and it wasn’t from her uncle and not through the direct channel. It was from the commission’s administrative office — Peng Yao’s desk, she identified the secondary seal — and it was a formal notice that the seasonal review structure was being modified. Effective the following cycle, direct correspondence between civilian physicians and commanding officers would route through the administrative secretariat for documentation purposes. All existing direct-channel correspondence would be archived under standard commission records.

She read it twice. She was very still for a moment. Mei Yun appeared in the doorway and saw her face and said nothing, which was the most useful thing she could have done. Shiyu set the letter on the table. She picked up her brush. She wrote, in the direct channel, to the General — not the administrative framing, not the commission language, plain and direct: I have received a formal notice from Peng Yao modifying the correspondence structure. I don’t know whether this has your authorisation. I am asking directly.

She sealed it. She sent it herself. She walked to the garrison in the early morning with the storm building in the west, the kind of cloud formation she recognised from three years of Qingzhou weather as serious rather than seasonal. On her return she stopped at Old Master Feng’s corner — he wasn’t there, the storm having driven him inside — and she thought about the direct-channel letter and the administrative notice and the deputy minister’s interests and the way Peng Yao had looked at the right side of the cabinet.

She thought: he isn’t interested in our methods.

She thought: he is interested in what the direct channel contains. What it implies. Who wrote to whom, and in what register, and what could be made of that in the right set of ears. The storm broke that afternoon while she was seeing patients. Rain came in the way it came to Qingzhou — decisively, without apology, the weight of a season releasing at once. The clinic’s drainage ran correctly. Her patients were sheltered. She treated a child’s fever and a carpenter’s hand laceration and the merchant woman’s headache with the focused competence of someone for whom the work was the thing, and the storm was outside and she was inside, and both of these were where they should be.

The General’s reply came two days later by relay rider, faster than any letter had ever come, which told her something about how he had received the question. It was two lines:

The notice wasn’t authorised by me. I have countermanded it. The direct channel remains unchanged.

Two lines. His private seal at the bottom, not the commission’s. Countermanded. Not reviewed, not considered — countermanded, which was a word that communicated that the notice hadn’t reached him before it went out, and that its existence was already being examined. She sat with this for a moment.

Then she wrote back, through the direct channel: Received. Thank you. And at the end, because she had decided three years ago that she was going to be honest and she wasn’t going to stop: The method changes Peng Yao proposed in his first month, and this attempt, point in the same direction. I believe he is trying to create a documented record that gives the appearance of impropriety between the commission’s physician and its commanding officer. I think you should know exactly what I believe his intention is.

She sealed it. She went to the garrison herself again. The storm had gentled to the steady rain that would last three days — the kind Qingzhou was built for, that filled the herb gardens and the river and the cisterns and made the city smell of wet stone and growth. She didn’t feel afraid. She felt, with the precision she had brought to clinical assessment for three years, that the situation had moved past a certain threshold. That Peng Yao had shown his direction. That whatever he intended, it was moving.

She went home. She ate dinner with her parents. Her father had his nose in the companion texts. Her mother asked careful questions about the commission visit and Shiyu answered them honestly, including — because her mother always knew anyway — that there had been a complication she was managing. Her mother looked at her with the direct loving attention of nineteen years.

“Are you safe?” she asked.

“Yes, the complication is administrative,” Shiyu said.

“Administrative. All right. Eat,” her mother said, in the tone of a woman who had been reading situations her whole life and whose definition of administrative was somewhat more generous than her daughter’s.

She ate. She slept. She didn’t know that in three weeks everything would change.

chapters.title: What Peng Yao Does
chapters.desc: A formal complaint names them both, and Peng Yao comes to the clinic to watch her hear about it.
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to inform you.” “Thank you for telling me. I will make a note of this visit in the clinic records.”
chapters.content:
The document arrived at the Emperor’s Censorate three weeks after the storm. She didn’t know this at the time. She would learn it afterward — from her uncle, from Chen Ye, from the General himself, in the fragmented way that truth assembled itself after an event that moved faster than any account of it. What she knew, in the week before the document arrived, was this: Peng Yao had been to the garrison three times. He had spoken with two officers she didn’t know. He had submitted a formal query to the commission administration asking for the complete record of direct correspondence between the clinic and the command.

Her uncle had refused the query on procedural grounds. The refusal was correct and properly documented. What Peng Yao had done, and with the patient competence of someone who had spent a career in administrative circles, was collect the outline of what the direct-channel correspondence existed without collecting its content. Volume. Frequency. The pattern of the two-week interval. The fact that the letters arrived in the General’s own hand. He hadn’t needed the content. He had the shape of it, and the shape was sufficient.

The document submitted to the Censorate was a formal concern — not an accusation, carefully framed, the language precise and neutral in the way of someone who understood that neutral framing was its own kind of weapon. It suggested that the Northern Army’s civilian medical commission had developed an administrative irregularity: a direct correspondence relationship between its supreme commanding officer and a civilian physician from the provinces, unusual in structure, sustained over an extended period, with a pattern that suggested the relationship had moved outside the commission’s intended scope.

It named her. It named him. It asked, with the measured neutrality of someone asking a question they already knew the answer to, whether the Emperor was aware of the nature of the relationship between the Northern Army’s General and the Qingcloud Medical Hall’s physician. She learned all of this later. In the present, on the morning the document was submitted, she was at the clinic seeing patients. The carpenter’s hand was healing correctly. Old Master Feng’s knee had responded well to the summer adjustment in the massage routine. A young woman from the east district had come in with a complaint that, after a careful assessment, she diagnosed as early-stage anaemia, manageable with diet and the iron-supplementing preparation she had been refining for two years.

She did her work. She was good at her work. The morning was ordinary. Then Peng Yao came to the clinic. He came in the middle of the day, which was unusual. He came alone, without administrative documentation, which was more unusual. He stood in the consultation room with the pleasant manner fully in place and looked at her with the expression of someone who had done the thing and was now watching the consequences arrive.

“I wanted to inform you that a concern has been submitted to the Censorate regarding the commission’s administrative structure. It is a procedural matter. I am sure it will be resolved without difficulty,” he said, in the measured voice of someone performing courtesy as a final gesture.

He paused.

“I am sure that the General will manage it efficiently. He manages most things efficiently,” he said, still pleasant.

Another pause, and something shifted beneath the pleasant surface — not cruelty, but the satisfaction of someone who had placed a thing correctly.

“The Emperor will be informed. These matters always go up the chain. I expect the commission itself will be unaffected. The physician’s involvement may need to be reviewed.”

She looked at him. In her previous life she had delivered serious diagnoses to hundreds of patients — had sat across that kind of table and said: this is what the situation is, and this is what it means. She had learned to read the people across from her: fear, denial, the held quality of someone who had already known. She read Peng Yao now and found something she hadn’t expected. Not the cold satisfaction of ambition achieved. Something more personal, and because of that, more dangerous.

He had been managing, she understood, the frustration of a competent man who had watched someone with less formal standing than he possessed be given influence he believed should have been distributed differently. The deputy minister’s recommendation had come with expectations. The commission’s success had been attributed, repeatedly and formally, to a provincial physician with no capital credentials. And the General — the Emperor’s nephew, the untouchable supreme commander — had chosen her, specifically and publicly, in a way that left no official room for the deputy minister’s candidate or Peng Yao’s ambitions.

Politics was only part of it. The rest was about being overlooked, and the specific, careful revenge of someone who had decided that the only available weapon was the appearance of impropriety. Fear didn’t come into it. She was, with cold clarity, furious.

“Thank you for telling me. I will make a note of this visit in the clinic records,” she said. Her voice was level.

Something moved in his expression — a fraction of something that wasn’t quite surprise.

“Of course,” he said, and left.

Mei Yun appeared in the doorway the moment the outer gate closed.

“I heard,” she said.

“I know.”

“Are you —”

Shiyu said, “Get me the correspondence log. And the commission filing record. I am going to document this conversation and every previous visit and every administrative query in the correct sequence, with dates and the exact content of each interaction, and it is going to be accurate and complete and it is going to exist before anything else happens.”

Mei Yun brought the correspondence log without another word. She wrote for two hours. She was thorough. Every visit, every question, every administrative filing, every look at the right side of the cabinet. The full record, in her handwriting, in the clinic documentation that had been continuous and unaltered for three years. When she finished she sealed it and wrote a cover letter to her uncle, through the garrison post, marked urgent.

Then she wrote, through the direct channel, to the General. She told him everything Peng Yao had said, in the order he had said it, with the same level and clinical detail she brought to medical reports: accurate, without annotation, giving it the weight it deserved and not more. She sealed that one and carried it to the garrison herself. On her walk back she passed the Jade Phoenix Inn. The gate lanterns were lit in the late afternoon. The city moved around her with its ordinary permanence.

She thought: he knew what he was doing when he did it. He chose the thing that would hurt, and the thing he chose was us. She breathed. She went home.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.desc: Four pages in his hand, and a promise to say it plainly to anyone who asks.
chapters.epigraph: There are things I want to say that have been waiting for the right time. — four pages, written without sleep
chapters.content:
The General’s reply came in two days, which was fast enough that she knew he hadn’t slept before he wrote it. It was four pages. She had never received four pages from him in the entire correspondence — the longest previous letter had been one and a half, and that had been the capital presentation follow-up with commission’s rules attached. Four pages, in his compressed careful hand, the characters closer together than usual in a way she associated with someone writing quickly.

He had contacted the Emperor. The concern at the Censorate had been reviewed at the imperial level within a day — the channel his position gave him was immediate and direct in a way that Peng Yao’s careful administrative framing hadn’t accounted for. The Emperor had reviewed the document. His response to the review, which her uncle had relayed, was characteristically terse: the commission’s structure is sound, the physician’s qualifications are a matter of documented record, and the administrative concern will be addressed through the appropriate channel.

The appropriate channel would be him. The General. The Emperor had, in his specific way, handed the matter back to the person most directly affected and most equipped to handle it. He wrote: I am returning to Qingzhou. Not for the seasonal review. I need to be present while this is addressed. He wrote: I should have acted on Peng Yao’s first intervention more directly. I monitored when I should have moved. That was my miscalculation. You will not bear the consequences of it.

He wrote, in the fourth page, in the language that wasn’t the commission language, not covered by administrative framing: I am aware that what he submitted names both of us and names it as something irregular. I want you to know that my response to the Emperor, and to any subsequent review, will be the same: there is nothing irregular about it. It is what it is. I will say so formally and without qualification if that is what the situation requires.

She read this section three times.

She thought: he will say it formally, to the Emperor, to anyone who asks. He has decided this already. He made this decision before he wrote this letter and the letter is the announcement of the decision, not the working-towards-it.

She thought: this is who he is. When he moves, he moves. She wrote back — four pages seemed right, for once — and she answered everything he had written, including the last section. She wrote: I know what it is. I would say the same, formally, if asked. I am not afraid of the situation. I am angry that he aimed at the clinic, because the clinic is not mine to risk the way my own standing is mine to risk. But the clinic’s records are three years of continuous documented work and they are sound. He cannot damage what is simply true.

She wrote: Come when you can. The review figures will be ready. And when the formal matter is settled I would like to talk — not through the channel, not in the consultation room. There are things I want to say that have been waiting for the right time and I think the right time is approaching. She sealed it. She slept. She slept well, which surprised her. The situation was real and serious and she was not minimising it. She was also, at the bottom of it, steady in a way she had not been steady at sixteen in a tent or at nineteen in the capital’s courtyard. The thing she had been building was not only the clinic. It was the ability to carry something large without being altered by it.

She woke before dawn, as she always did. She made tea. She did the morning preparations. She didn’t know that in two days everything would break in a direction no one had anticipated.

chapters.title: The Riverbank
chapters.desc: A child falls at the second bend. She goes alone. Peng Yao is waiting.
chapters.epigraph: “Move aside, please.” — Yun Shiyu, at the second bend, with her bag
chapters.content:
The emergency came from the western district. A child had fallen from the bridge abutment during the afternoon — the old stone bridge at the river’s second bend, the one the river district children used as a jumping platform in high summer and which the city had been meaning to fence for as long as anyone could remember. The fall hadn’t been the river but the abutment’s edge, and the injury was serious: head wound, loss of consciousness reported by witnesses, the sequence of events that meant she needed to move immediately.

Mei Yun was with another patient. Shiyu took her bag and went alone. She had done this before, would do it again, the situation required speed and she had speed. The western district was a quarter of an hour on foot from the clinic. She went quickly, not running — running on Qingzhou’s stone streets risked exactly the kind of fall she was about to treat — but at the fast deliberate pace of someone who knew how to move efficiently over familiar ground.

The bridge was crowded when she arrived: river workers, neighbours, two soldiers from the garrison who had responded to the commotion. The child was conscious — she assessed this from ten paces away, the small body responding to voice, which was the most important thing. Head wound, left temple, bleeding significantly but the quality of the blood flow was not arterial. Possible concussion. She needed to establish responsiveness. She went to work.

She didn’t notice Peng Yao at first. She was focused on the child — establishing the injury extent, keeping the small body still, talking to the mother who had arrived and was very frightened and needed someone to be calm. Shiyu was calm. She had done this, in different shapes, a thousand times in two lifetimes. She became aware of him when she stood to direct one of the garrison soldiers in moving the child — and found him at the edge of the bridge crowd, not watching the child, watching her.

With an expression she didn’t have time to read in full. She directed the soldier. She walked beside the child to the nearest house with a suitable room, where she could continue the examination properly. She didn’t look back at Peng Yao. She was with the child for an hour. The concussion assessment was thorough — she didn’t rush it, the stakes were exactly as high as they appeared. The wound was cleaned and closed with the care she gave every closure, regardless of the setting. The child was responsive, tracking correctly, no sign of bleeding inside the skull. She gave the mother specific instructions for the night watch, wrote them down on a slip of paper, made her repeat them back. The child would be well.

She gathered her supplies. She stepped back out onto the river district street. Peng Yao was there. He was standing at the intersection of the river path and the street, alone, and his expression had changed from what she had seen at the bridge. The pleasant surface wasn’t entirely in place. What was beneath it — she hadn’t seen this before, not this fully — was the look of a man who had lost something he had been counting on, and who had decided, in the way of people who had lost control of a situation and had nothing left to manage, to do the last available thing.

He said, “The Bureau accepted the concern. The General’s response has been noted. But noted does not mean resolved. The commission’s future is not certain. What the physician does next will be observed.” No preamble.

She looked at him. The river was loud at this part of its bend, the summer water high.

“I am going back to my clinic,” she said.

He said, “I would suggest that maintaining a very public distance from the command would help resolve the situation more quickly. For the clinic. For the commission. For the General’s standing with the Emperor.”

She understood immediately what this was. Not a threat in the direct sense — nothing that could be reported as a threat. A suggestion. The kind that arrived dressed as advice and functioned as pressure, and the pressure was aimed precisely at the place he had calculated was the softest: the possibility that maintaining what she had with the General would cost him. She was very still. She was also standing two paces from the river at the second bend’s path edge, and Peng Yao was between her and the street back to the clinic, and the afternoon had gone grey in the way of summer evenings before a second rain, and the garrison soldiers who had been at the bridge had dispersed.

She said: “Move aside, please.”

He stepped towards her instead — not threateningly, not with raised hands, just the step of a man reducing distance, and she registered this with the clinical clarity of someone who had assessed physical situations in emergency medicine and understood that the space between being in danger and not being in danger was sometimes a single breath. She stepped back. The path edge was where she hadn’t quite assessed it to be.

She didn’t fall. She was pushed. She wouldn’t be certain of this later — or rather, she would be certain and would acknowledge that certainty to herself and to no one else for a long time, because certainty and proof weren’t the same thing. What she knew, in the one clear instant of the bank giving way: the pressure against her shoulder from behind, deliberate and specific, not her own momentum, not the earth, the intent.

Then the river. The water was fast at the second bend. She had known this abstractly — she had lived in Qingzhou for nineteen years and walked the river path a thousand times and she knew the second bend was fast. Knowing and being in it were different things. She didn’t panic. She had done drowning survival training in her previous life and her body remembered it, the lateral sweep, the surface seeking, the breathe when you can and don’t fight the current. The water was cold for summer. Her bag was gone — she felt the strap tear away, which was correct, the weight would have been the end of it. She kicked towards what she could identify as surface.

She surfaced once. She had a breath and a bearing. The current was taking her east. East was towards the river district’s lower bend, which was — she had half a breath to calculate — the section before the river narrowed into the gorge. She needed the south bank. She needed it within the next hundred paces. She swam. The cloud-embroidered pouch tore loose from her sash. The jade hairpin from her grandmother went with the current. She was aware of these losses in the background of the absolute present-tense emergency of staying alive and moving towards the bank.

She almost made it. The rock at the gorge’s entry caught her shoulder — a hard, spinning impact that turned her in the water, and she lost the bearing, and the current had her, and she was going into the gorge, and the last clear thing she knew before the roar of the water took everything else was: the General will look for me. She held onto that. She went under.

chapters.title: What the General Knows
chapters.desc: The report reaches him on the road: no body recovered.
chapters.epigraph: “We are not stopping for the night. We move now.” — the General, on the northern road
chapters.content:
He received the report on the fourth day. He had been in transit — the letter about his return to Qingzhou had been real and he had moved on it immediately, because that was how he operated: decide, move. He was two days out from Qingzhou when the first dispatch caught him. Not through the commission channel. Through the garrison’s emergency post, from Chen Ye, who had ridden ahead and been in Qingzhou for six hours when the report came in.

The physician from the Qingcloud Medical Hall. Riverbank incident. Western district, second bend. One witness. No body recovered. He read the dispatch once. He read it again. Chen Ye, writing in the flat language of a man reporting a situation: No body recovered isn’t confirmed. The river’s speed at the gorge entry makes recovery uncertain. The search has begun. I thought you should know before you arrived.

He folded the dispatch. He put it in his inner coat. He said, in the voice he used for situations that required absolute operational clarity: “We are not stopping for the night. We move now.”

No one questioned this. He arrived in Qingzhou before dawn. The search was active. Two garrison teams, river district workers who knew the water, her father who hadn’t slept — Yun Chengde, standing at the second bend looking like a man whose entire framework for what was possible had been violently restructured and hadn’t yet found a new shape to occupy. Her mother was at the house, with the composed stillness of someone managing something enormous by managing the smallest things: the tea, the lamp, the gate left open.

He went to the river first. Chen Ye briefed him on the bank. One witness — a river worker who had been at a distance, had seen the struggle of someone in the water, had raised the alarm. Peng Yao had been at the scene and had left before the garrison arrived. This last detail was delivered with the flatness of a man who knew what it meant. He stood at the bank and looked at the second bend and the gorge entry. He assessed the current. He thought about physics — speed, direction, the volume of the summer water, what it did to a person. He thought about her — the steadiness in her hands, the way she had swum towards the bank in his reconstruction of it because that was what she would do, she wouldn’t panic, she would calculate. He thought about the private terror of not knowing if calculation had been enough.

“Who saw Peng Yao last,” he said.

“The witness. At the bank. He left before the alarm was raised. He returned to his lodging afterward. He has not left since.” Chen Ye paused.

He was quiet for a moment. “Keep him there. Do not let him know he is being kept. Do not let him leave the city,” he said.

“Yes, General.”

“The search continues. All available personnel. The gorge exit and the lower bend particularly — if she cleared the gorge she would have come out on the north or east bank. The current pattern favours east.”

“Yes, General.”

He looked at the river. He had spent every year since he was fifteen learning to be the man who didn’t let his face say what he felt, because showing what you felt in his world was giving ammunition to people who would use it. He had been excellent at this. He had been, some part of him acknowledged, too excellent at it for too long. He wasn’t, in this moment, managing his expression.

There was no one to manage it for. Chen Ye had seen it, but Chen Ye wasn’t the kind of person who needed it managed for him. He went to speak with her father. Yun Chengde was a gentle man and a scholar and he had spent fifty-five years in a world where governance and medicine and the gentle arts of administration were the substance of life. He wasn’t equipped, by experience or temperament, for what had happened to his daughter.

He was, the General saw when he reached him, trying. He was standing at the second bend watching the search team work with the stillness of someone who had decided the only available thing was to be present at the place. He had his notebook in his hand. He wasn’t writing in it. He was simply holding it. The General stood beside him for a moment. He had words. He had many words — the operational assessment, the probabilities, the search plan he had implemented and which was as thorough as he could make it. He had the language of a commander who had told families things before and had learned that honesty was more useful than comfort because comfort that was false made things worse.

He said: “She knows how to fight for it. She has been doing it her whole life.”

Yun Chengde looked at him. And something in his face — the grief-masked, sleep-deprived, slightly bewildered face of a man who had always known his daughter was more than he entirely understood — shifted into something else. Something that recognised, in those specific words, a person who also knew her. He nodded once. They stood at the second bend together until the dawn came up over the river hills.

chapters.title: Dead or Alive
chapters.desc: He finds her hairpin below the gorge, and rides to the Emperor for permission to cross the border.
chapters.epigraph: “Bring her back, Lingyun.” — the Emperor
chapters.content:
He gave the situation three days. Not because he believed she was dead — he didn’t, and this wasn’t the denial of a man refusing to accept what the evidence suggested, but the considered assessment of a man who had spent thirteen years reading situations and trusted his reading. She had been close to the south bank. She was strong and calm and didn’t panic and he had seen her face situations that would have broken people who had less of her particular clarity. Three days meant: the search has time to be thorough, and then I move.

The search was thorough. He directed it himself, pulling teams he wouldn’t normally have pulled, using the authority of his position in a way that communicated to everyone involved the weight of this situation.

On the second day he dealt with Peng Yao. He did this formally, in the garrison’s administrative chamber, with documentation and witnesses and the complete procedural structure of a military inquiry. He was precise. He gave Peng Yao every opportunity to characterise the riverbank interaction as he chose. He documented the characterisation. He documented the witness account. He documented the timeline: where Peng Yao had been, when, what he had done before and after. He documented Peng Yao’s administrative record at the commission: the initial method review challenge, the attempted correspondence channel modification, the Censorate submission. He was thorough. He was, he intended to be, irrefutable.

Peng Yao’s pleasant manner held through the first hour. It didn’t hold through the second. What emerged wasn’t a confession — a man like Peng Yao would never confess directly — but the pattern of someone whose constructed explanations didn’t survive the application of sequential, careful logic. He became defensive in the way of someone who hadn’t expected the opposition to be quite this prepared. He had made his career in administrative circles where friction could be managed by relationship and surface, and he was encountering someone for whom surface wasn’t a relevant consideration.

The inquiry concluded. He submitted the full record to the Emperor through the formal channel. His personal letter to the Emperor was brief. He had written it once and not revised it:

The evidence points to one conclusion. I am submitting it for your review. I am not asking for a particular outcome, only that the review be complete. I trust your judgment on the formal consequence. On my own response to this man and what he did, I will ask your permission to act personally.

The Emperor’s reply came in a day. The Emperor had, characteristically, read everything and formed a complete view before responding:

The formal consequence will be administered through the Censorate. He will not be in a position to do this again. Your permission is granted. Do what you need to do — I would suggest doing it in a way that is memorable but leaves no diplomatic complications. And Lingyun — find her.

He found the jade hairpin on the third day. A fishing family at the lower gorge exit. They had found it snagged in their net two days before — small, jade, carved with the cloud motif. He knew it. He had seen it at the capital, pressed into her hair by her mother’s hand. He held it in his palm and looked at it. She had cleared the gorge. She had come out on the east side.

East of the gorge was forty li of riverside terrain before the first significant settlement — and beyond the first settlement, the border region. And beyond the border region, which was administered but porous in the summer season when the high water changed the traditional crossing points —he looked at the map in his mind. His search teams had already reached the border marker on the east bank, and there they had stopped. Imperial soldiers didn’t cross it. He wouldn’t order them to.

He rode for the capital that night. He changed horses at every relay station and was in the palace on the second evening. This audience was, by the Emperor’s own arrangement, not to be rushed. The Emperor sat with the letter from Qingzhou and looked at his nephew and said, in the tone he used when he had already arrived somewhere and was waiting for the other person to catch up:

“You want to go across.”

“The jade hairpin places her at the gorge exit on the east bank. The current would have carried her to the settlement at the border marking, or past it into the border region. If she is alive she is somewhere along that line.”

“If she is alive,” the Emperor said.

“She is alive.” He said this without qualification. He was aware of how it sounded. He didn’t revise it.

The Emperor looked at him for a long moment with the assessing attention of a man who had been watching people for thirty years and had learned to tell the difference between certainty and desperation. What he saw, apparently, was certainty.

“You cannot enter the border region officially. Not with your title. The political implications alone —” he said.

He said, “Not officially. One officer, in civilian clothes. Following the river east. Looking for a physician from a provincial clinic who was swept downstream. There is no political implication in a private individual following a river.”

A pause.

“You are not a private individual.”

“I will be for this purpose.”

The Emperor was quiet for a moment. He looked at his nephew — at the controlled stillness, the jaw set, the dark eyes that weren’t performing patience but had none left on this subject — and he thought about a young general who had never, in thirteen years, asked him for a personal thing, only professional authority, only resources for campaigns, only the structures of a military mandate. He thought about what it meant that this was the personal thing.

“Chen Ye goes with you,” the Emperor said.

“Yes.”

“You are travelling as — what? Merchants are too obvious in the border settlements. Physicians —”

A brief silence.

“Physicians. How appropriate,” the Emperor said again, with something that wasn’t quite amusement and was definitely something.

“Travelling scholars. It holds in the settlement zones. We carry enough documentation,” he said.

“Travelling scholars. I will have the travel documents prepared. You will have full imperial authority the moment you return to this side of the border, but on the other side you are a private individual following a river. Bring her back, Lingyun.” The Emperor picked up his brush. He signed the documents. He held them out.

He took the documents. “I intend to,” he said.

chapters.title: The Letter at the Border Post
chapters.desc: At the flooded border, a letter in charcoal and a pouch embroidered with clouds.
chapters.epigraph: “She says not to let anyone cross for her.” “I would point out that you are anyone.” — Chen Ye, at the border post
chapters.content:
He rode south out of the capital with the travel documents inside his coat and Chen Ye half a length behind him, and neither of them spoke until the first relay station.

At the station Chen Ye handed him a bowl of soup, waited until he had drunk half of it, and said, “You should sleep for two hours.”

“No.”

“Then I will sleep for two hours, and you can watch the horses.”

He didn’t answer that. Chen Ye slept for two hours on a bench by the stable wall. The General sat on the step outside with the jade hairpin in his hand and watched the horses, and when Chen Ye woke they rode on. They came back through Qingzhou at dawn on the eleventh day. He didn’t stop at the governor’s residence. He did stop at the second bend, because Yun Chengde was there, as he had been every morning, standing on the bank with his notebook. The General told him three things in the order that mattered: that the Emperor had given permission, that he was going across himself, and that he would send word the moment he knew anything at all.

Her father listened to all of it. Then he took off his outer coat — a good coat, the governor’s coat, with the embroidered collar — and held it out.

“She’ll be cold. If you find her. The river is cold even in summer,” he said.

The General took the coat and tied it behind his saddle. Neither of them said anything else. There was nothing else that would have helped. The border marker stood forty li downstream, at the place where the river came out of the hills and spread wide and brown across a gravel plain. There was a settlement there of perhaps thirty houses, a ferry landing with no ferry, and a small post with two clerks and a flag. The search teams had camped beside the post for a week. They stood when the General rode in and saw what he was wearing — a scholar’s plain grey robe, no insignia, no armour — and, being soldiers, very carefully didn’t mention it.

The ford was under water. A man could see where it ought to be: two posts on this bank, two on the far bank, and between them a stretch of river moving fast enough to roll stones along the bottom. The far bank was another country on paper. In practice it was hill farms and fishing villages that paid tax to whoever came asking and had a strong opinion of neither side.

“How long since the water was low enough to cross?” he asked the senior clerk.

“Twenty days, sir. Twenty-two.”

The clerk was a thin young man with ink on his cuffs who had clearly been told who the scholar in grey really was and was trying not to stare at him.

“It usually drops at the end of the eighth month. We’re close.”

“Has anything come across?”

“Nothing by the ford. A salt trader came over the hill path two days ago. From the villages on the other side. He left a letter for the post to send on. It’s for the Governor of Qingzhou, so I put it with the next bag for the garrison, but the bag doesn’t go until —” The clerk hesitated.

The General was already walking towards the post. The letter was in the bag under the window, between a tax return and a complaint about a goat. It was folded small and tied with a strip of blue cloth, and there was no seal, because the person who wrote it had nothing to seal it with. Something else was tied into the cloth with it. He knew what it was before he had the knot undone.

A small pouch, faded silk, embroidered with clouds. River water had stiffened it and sun had dried it pale. One corner of the stitching had come loose. He had watched her press her fingers to that pouch for nearly four years. In the medical tent, when the conversation went somewhere she hadn’t planned for. At the inn, when she thought no one was looking. In the capital, once, in the second before she walked into the presentation hall. She did it when there was something she couldn’t say. He had never asked her about it. He had simply known, the way he knew which of his officers rubbed his jaw before he lied.

He opened the letter. It was written in charcoal, on the back of a page torn from a trader’s account book, and the characters were cramped and slanted because the writer had been lying down when she wrote them. But they were hers. He would have known them anywhere.

To Yun Chengde, Governor of Qingzhou.
I am alive. I am at the fishing village of Wide Water, a day and a half by the hill path from the border marker, on the east bank. My left shoulder came out of its socket in the river; it is back in. I had a fever; it is gone. The people here pulled me out of the water and have been kind to me.
The ford is closed until the water drops. Please don’t let anyone cross for me in high water. I will come home as soon as I can walk the hill path.
The pouch is so you know this is from me.
— Shiyu

He read it once. He read it again. Then he sat down on the clerk’s stool, because his legs had made the decision before he had, and he held the letter in both hands and didn’t move for some time. Chen Ye came into the post, looked at him, and looked at the letter. He didn’t ask. He went back out and told the soldiers to stand down and the search teams to strike camp, and then he came back in and waited.

“She’s alive. She’s at a place called Wide Water. She put her shoulder back in herself,” the General said at last. His voice didn’t sound like his own.

“Of course she did,” said Chen Ye. He sounded perfectly calm. He also had to turn and look out of the window for a moment, and the General let him.

“She says not to cross in high water.”

Chen Ye looked at the ford, which was roaring, and then at the General, who was looking at the ford.

“She says not to let anyone cross for her. I would point out that you are anyone,” Chen Ye said carefully.

There had been a time — not long ago, a few months — when he would have weighed the river against the risk and crossed anyway, and called it a decision. He thought about the letter she had written him in the summer. I would prefer to be in possession of relevant information at the time it becomes relevant. I want you to understand mine. And his own answer: I will not manage around you again.

She had told him what she wanted. In charcoal, lying down, with her shoulder freshly put back.

“Find the salt trader. We take the hill path,” he said.

The salt trader was a broad, cheerful man called Tuo, with a laugh like a dropped pot and two mules that hated each other. He was in the settlement’s only tea house, and when he understood that the two scholars wanted to go to Wide Water, that night, he laughed his dropped-pot laugh and said it was a day and a half on foot and nobody walked the hill path in the dark. When the General put a silver ingot on the table, Tuo stopped laughing and said that, now he thought about it, the moon was nearly full.

They left an hour after sunset. The path climbed out of the river plain into steep, terraced hills where tea bushes grew in rows and dogs barked at them from every farm. Tuo talked the whole way. He talked about salt prices and his mules and his wife’s brother, and somewhere past midnight, when the General had stopped listening, he started talking about the river doctor.

“Pulled her out of the shallows below Wide Water, Old Nai did. She and her son. Thought she was dead. She had a bruise on her face like a plum. Two days later she’s sitting up telling Old Nai’s son how to pull her own arm. Then she’s up and walking. Then she’s lancing the headman’s hand. Now every child in the village follows her around like ducks. You’re her family?” Tuo shook his head. He looked sideways at the General.

“No,” said the General.

Tuo waited.

“Not yet,” said the General, and Chen Ye, walking behind them, made a small sound that might have been a cough.

They slept for three hours in a shepherd’s hut at the top of the ridge, because Tuo said the mules wouldn’t go on otherwise and Chen Ye said the General wouldn’t be able to go on otherwise, and the General, who hadn’t slept properly in eleven days, didn’t argue with either of them. He slept with the pouch in his hand. They came down into Wide Water in the late afternoon of the second day.

It was exactly what its name promised. The river came out of the hills and opened into a broad, slow pool, with reed beds along the edges and fishing boats pulled up on the mud. The village sat on the slope above it — forty or fifty houses of dark wood and grey stone, drying racks of fish, chickens in the lane, smoke from cooking fires. A few women were mending nets in a yard. A dog came out to bark at them and then thought better of it.

He heard the children before he saw them. A whole flock of them, shrieking and laughing, came running down the main lane towards the river, and in the middle of them, walking more slowly, with her left arm bound against her body in a sling made from a fishing net and a dozen small hands holding on to her skirt, was a woman in a borrowed blue jacket that was too big for her.

She was thinner. There was a fading bruise along her cheekbone, yellow at the edges. Her hair was tied up with a strip of cloth instead of a hairpin. She was saying something to the children in a dialect he didn’t know, and they were laughing at the way she said it, and she was laughing too. A little girl near the front, running backward to look at her, caught her heel on a stone and pitched towards the ground.

A hand shot out — her right hand, quick and sure — and caught the child by the back of her jacket and set her upright on her feet before she had even finished falling. He stood still for one breath. Then he moved.

chapters.title: The River Doctor
chapters.desc: Thirteen days on the far side of the river, and one question she can’t stop asking: who was behind her?
chapters.epigraph: “Look where you’re going, little goose.” — Old Nai, Wide Water
chapters.content:
She didn’t remember the end of the gorge. She remembered the rock and the spin and the roar, and the thought she had held onto as she went under. After that there was only cold and dark and a sense of being thrown about inside something enormous that didn’t know she was there. At some point there had been wood under her arms — a branch, or part of a tree — and she had held it because her body wouldn’t let go. At some point there had been light.

The next thing she knew for certain was a smell: smoke, fish, and the bitter green of some herb being boiled. Then a ceiling of dark beams, very low, with nets hanging from it. Then a face. An old woman, brown and creased as a walnut, with no front teeth, peering down at her and saying something in a dialect so thick that Shiyu understood only one word of it, which was alive.

“Yes. Thank you. Where —” Shiyu said. Her voice came out as a croak.

Then she tried to move, and her left shoulder told her a great deal very quickly, and for a while she didn’t ask anything at all. The old woman was called Old Nai. Her son, who was called Second Son by everyone including his mother, had pulled Shiyu out of the reeds at the edge of the wide pool below the village, two mornings before. They had thought she was a drowned body until she coughed. Old Nai had stripped off her wet clothes, wrapped her in a quilt, and poured hot broth into her a spoonful at a time while she lay there not waking up. All of this Shiyu worked out slowly, over the first afternoon, from gestures and repetition and the handful of words in the hill dialect that were close enough to Qingzhou speech to guess at.

The shoulder was dislocated. She knew that the moment she was clear-headed enough to examine it with her good hand: the flat, wrong shape at the top of the arm, the head of the bone sitting forward where it shouldn’t be. Two days out of the socket. Every hour made it harder to put back. She couldn’t do it alone. She explained what she needed to Second Son with her right hand and the few words they shared and, eventually, by drawing it with a finger in the ash of the hearth. He was a big, quiet man of about thirty who mended boats, and he looked at the drawing for a long time with deep reluctance before he nodded.

She lay on the floor. Old Nai folded a quilt into a long roll and passed it under Shiyu’s arm and around her chest, and held both ends, and braced her feet against the doorframe. Second Son took Shiyu’s wrist in his two large hands.

“Slowly. Slowly. Keep pulling. Do not stop when I make noise,” Shiyu said. She had taught him the word for slowly an hour earlier.

He pulled. She made noise. He looked as if he wanted to stop and she said “Slowly” through her teeth and he kept going, steady, the way he would draw a boat up a bank, and somewhere in the long burning stretch of it she felt the muscles give and the bone slide and then a deep, dull clunk that she felt in her jaw. She lay on the floor and breathed. Second Son sat back on his heels, grey in the face. Old Nai said something that was clearly a prayer.

“Good, that was very good. Thank you,” Shiyu said. And then, because her body had been waiting for permission, she cried a little, with her face turned to the wall. Old Nai patted her hair and didn’t ask why.

The fever came that night and stayed for two days. She knew what it was — the wound on her scalp where the rock had caught her, river water in it, her body worn down to nothing. She talked Old Nai through what she needed: boiled water, salt, clean cloth, the willow bark she could see drying on the rack. She drank everything she was given. She didn’t let herself be frightened, because fear wouldn’t help and she had nothing to spare.

In the fever, she went back over the riverbank. She did it the way she would go back over a case that had gone wrong — carefully, in order, refusing to skip anything. Peng Yao at the corner of the path, in front of her, between her and the street. His face. His hands, open, held a little out from his sides, the way a man holds his hands when he wants you to see they are empty. The step he took towards her. The step she took back.

And then the push. Low on her back, below her shoulder blade, flat and hard and meant. From behind. She went over it again and again in the hot dark, and every time it came out the same. Peng Yao had been in front of her. Both his hands had been in front of her, where she could see them. He had made sure she could see them. So someone else had been behind her.

On the second night of the fever, an image came to her that she didn’t trust: a man’s hand, the back of it, with a shiny pink scar across the knuckles like an old burn. She didn’t know where it had come from. She thought perhaps it was the hand of the garrison soldier she had asked to lift the child at the bridge — she had watched his hands as he picked the little boy up, because she had been worried he would jar the neck. But she had been feverish when she remembered it, and she knew exactly how much a fevered memory was worth.

She put it carefully to one side. Not thrown away. Labelled, the way she would label a sample she wasn’t yet sure of. The fever broke on the fifth morning after the river. On the sixth, she sat up. On the seventh, a salt trader came to Old Nai’s door — a big, loud, cheerful man with two mules — and she understood, from Old Nai’s pointing, that he was going over the hills towards the border marker in the morning.

He had paper: a battered account book. He had charcoal. She tore out a page and wrote to her father, lying on her side on the quilt because sitting up for long still made the room tilt. She wrote what had happened and where she was. She wrote that the ford was closed. She thought about the people who would read it — her father, her uncle, and one other person who would certainly read it whatever its address — and she added: Please do not let anyone cross for me in high water.

She knew him. She knew what he would want to do. She wrote it anyway, because she wanted him to know what she wanted.

Then she needed something to prove the letter was hers. She had nothing left. The river had taken her bag, her shoes, her hairpin, her grandmother’s hairpin.
