She had the borrowed jacket and the quilt and, still knotted into the sash that Old Nai had dried by the fire, the cloud-embroidered pouch. It had held its stitches through the gorge. She didn’t know how. Her mother had made it for her when she was six — the first year after the fever, when her daughter woke up strange and quiet and too clever and her mother didn’t know what had happened to her and loved her anyway. It was the only thing Shiyu owned that had no use. She had pressed her fingers to it ten thousand times.

She tied it into the letter with a strip of blue cloth and gave it to the trader, and told him, in the five words of hill dialect she had by then, that it was important. He nodded very seriously and put it inside his shirt. After he had gone, she found that her hand kept going to her sash, to the place where the pouch wasn’t. She let it. There was no one to see.

On the eighth day, the headman of Wide Water came to Old Nai’s house holding his right hand in his left. It was swollen to the wrist, red and hot and shiny, from a fish-hook wound three days old. Old Nai had told the whole village by then that the woman from the river knew medicine. The headman didn’t look. He looked to be in too much pain to care.

She lanced the hand with a fishing knife she boiled first, drained it, packed it with salt and boiled cloth, and told him through Old Nai to come back every morning. He came back the next morning, and the swelling was down, and he looked at her differently. After that, people came. A fisherman with a cough. A baby with a rash. A boy who had stepped on a nail. A pregnant woman, the headman’s daughter, round and anxious, who held Shiyu’s good hand very tightly while Shiyu felt the shape of the baby through her belly and didn’t like what she found. She did what she could with one arm and the herbs on Old Nai’s rack and the things Second Son fetched from the hillside when she drew them for him. She learned the words for pain and where and better and tomorrow. She learned twelve children’s names.

The children decided she was theirs. They followed her from house to house. They laughed at her accent. They called her something that she eventually understood to mean the river doctor, and they wanted to hear, over and over, how she had come down the river on a tree. She told them, in very bad dialect, with a great deal of waving of her good arm. It got bigger every time.

At night she lay on Old Nai’s floor and counted. A day and a half for the trader to cross the hills to the border post — longer, Old Nai said, because he had salt to sell in every village on the way. Then however long a letter took to go from a border post to Qingzhou. Then — what? Her father would read it. Her mother. Mei Yun. And he would have been told by now. He had been on the road to Qingzhou when she fell. He would have arrived to find her gone.

She thought about his face reading the report, and couldn’t bear it, and thought about it anyway. She didn’t think: he will come. She thought: he will want to. She had asked him not to cross in high water. She didn’t know whether he would listen. She thought he would try very hard to, and she found, lying in the dark with the river sounds outside, that she loved him for it so much that it hurt worse than the shoulder had.

On the thirteenth day after the river, in the late afternoon, she walked back from the headman’s house with the sling made from a piece of old net cutting into her neck and seven children holding on to her skirt. The headman’s daughter had been having pains since noon. They weren’t the right pains yet, but they would be by night. Shiyu was thinking about the baby’s position, and what she could do with one arm, and whether the village midwife would let her try.

Little Ke, the smallest, was running backward in front of her, telling a long story about a goose. She caught her heel on a stone.

Shiyu’s hand went out without her deciding. She caught the child by the back of her jacket and set her on her feet and said, in her terrible dialect, “Look where you’re going, little goose.”

The children shrieked with laughter. She looked up, smiling, over their heads.

At the bottom of the lane, where the path came down from the hills, two men in plain grey scholars’ robes had stopped beside a salt trader’s mules. One of them was standing perfectly still. Then he wasn’t.

chapters.title: A Lamp for the Midwife
chapters.desc: He finds her. Then he holds a lamp all night while she delivers a baby with one arm.
chapters.epigraph: “Where I tell you. For as long as it takes. And not faint.” — instructions for holding a lamp
chapters.content:
He didn’t run. Afterwards she thought that was the most like him of anything he did that day. He walked up the lane at a pace that was almost a run and wasn’t one, and the children scattered out of his way like hens, and he stopped a single pace from her and looked at her. She had seen his face do a great many things over four years, all of them small. She had learned to read the corner of his mouth and the set of his jaw and the half-breath before he answered a question he hadn’t expected. She had built a whole language out of the little he let show.

None of it was any use now. Nothing was being held back. He looked like a man who hadn’t slept in two weeks and had walked over a mountain in the dark and had just found the one thing he had been afraid he would never see again, and he didn’t try to make it look like anything else.

“You told them not to cross,” he said. His voice was rough.

“Did you?”

“We came over the hill.”

She let out a breath she seemed to have been holding for thirteen days.

“Good. That’s — good,” she said.

He reached inside his robe and took out something small, and held it out to her on his open palm. The pouch. She took it with her good hand. The silk was stiff and faded and one corner of the stitching had come loose. Her fingers closed over it and pressed, the way they always did, before she had decided anything at all.

“You do that, when there is something you cannot say,” he said.

She looked up at him. “How long have you known that?”

“Since the tent.”

Since she was sixteen. Since the interrogation, when she had stood in front of him and his five officers and told the truth because she couldn’t think of a lie good enough. He had been watching her hands even then. She had been steady for thirteen days. She had put her own shoulder back and sweated out a fever on a stranger’s floor and lanced a headman’s hand with a fishing knife. She had been steady because there had been nobody to be anything else in front of.

Now there was. She stepped forward and put her forehead against his chest, and stood there with the pouch crushed in her hand and her bad arm trapped between them, and shook. Not crying, exactly. Just shaking, the way a body does when it finally sets something heavy down. His hand came up and rested on the back of her head. It wasn’t quite steady either.

“I’m here,” he said into her hair. That was all. He said it twice.

Behind them, in the lane, a dozen children stood in a solid, staring silence.

Chen Ye cleared his throat. “Who would like to see a scholar do a trick with a copper coin?” he said to them, in very careful Qingzhou speech that they couldn’t possibly understand.

They didn’t understand the words. They understood the coin. He led them off down the lane towards the river with the air of a man who had done this before, and Tuo followed with the mules, laughing his dropped-pot laugh. Shiyu stayed where she was for a while longer. Then she stepped back, wiped her face with the heel of her good hand, and looked at him properly.

“You look terrible,” she said.

“I have not slept.”

“For how long?”

He considered this. “Some time.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have. Your shoulder.” His eyes went to the bruise on her cheek, the sling, the borrowed jacket. Something moved in his jaw.

“Second Son pulled it and I told him not to stop. It’s back in. It’ll be weak for a month. I had a fever. It’s gone. I’m thin and my head hurts in the mornings. That’s everything. I promise.” She watched him not ask the next question.

He nodded slowly, as if he was filing each item somewhere he could find it again.

“Your father sent his coat. He said you would be cold,” he said.

That nearly undid her a second time. She pressed the pouch again instead.

“Is he —”

“He goes to the second bend every morning. Your mother keeps the gate open. Mei Yun has kept the clinic running. They are all well. They will be better when they see you.”

“Then we should go. Tomorrow. At first light,” she said.

She saw him start to say now and decide not to.

“Tomorrow. Tonight you will eat something, and sleep,” he agreed.

“Tonight, I can’t,” she said.

She told him about the headman’s daughter while they walked up the lane. The baby was lying wrong — bottom first, not head first — and the pains had started at noon. The village midwife was a sensible woman who had delivered half of Wide Water, and she was frightened, because a baby that came the wrong way round was a baby that often didn’t live, and sometimes took its mother with it.

Shiyu said, “I may be able to turn it. Before the birth gets too far. If not, I know what to do when it comes the wrong way. But I’ve only got one arm, and the midwife doesn’t trust me yet, and I need light. Their lamps are fish-oil. They’re dim and they smoke.”

He was quiet for a few steps. “What do you need that I can do?” he said.

He didn’t say you should rest, or let someone else. She had known he wouldn’t say those things, and still it went through her like warmth.

“Hold a lamp. Where I tell you. For as long as it takes. And not faint,” she said.

“I have never fainted.”

“You’ve never been in a birthing room.”

“No,” he admitted.

The midwife didn’t want a man in the room. The headman didn’t want a stranger in the room. Shiyu stood in the doorway with her arm in a sling and said, in her five words of dialect and a great deal of pointing, that she needed light and she needed hands she trusted, and that this man had sat up with wounded soldiers through worse nights than this one and was very good at holding things still. All of which was true.

The midwife looked at him for a long moment. He looked back with a face so plainly serious that she threw up her hands and let him in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He held the lamp for nine hours. He held it where she told him, high and steady, and moved it when she said move, and didn’t look away from anything. He watched her kneel beside the bed and lay her good hand on the girl’s belly and push, slow and patient, for a very long time, while the girl cried and the midwife muttered and the baby didn’t turn. He watched her stop, and breathe, and try once more, and fail again, and say calmly to the midwife, in her broken dialect, that the baby was coming the wrong way round and they would do it that way, together.

He watched the midwife decide to trust her. It was past midnight when the birth began in earnest and nearly dawn when it ended. Most of it he wouldn’t have been able to describe afterwards. He remembered her voice — low, even, never hurried, talking the girl through each pain in words the girl understood less and less and needed more and more. He remembered her one good hand moving quickly and surely. He remembered the moment, near the end, when the baby’s body was born and the head wasn’t, and the room went very still. Shiyu said one short sharp word to the midwife, and they did something together with their hands that he didn’t follow.

And then there was a small, slippery, furious creature in the midwife’s arms, and it opened its mouth and screamed. He found that he had to put the lamp down on the shelf. The midwife laughed and cried at the same time. The headman’s daughter sobbed. Outside the door the headman, who had been pacing the yard all night, let out a shout that woke every dog in Wide Water.

Shiyu sat back on her heels on the earth floor. Her hair had come down. There was blood to her elbow. She looked up at him, and her face was grey with tiredness and completely, simply happy.

“A girl. Both of them alive,” she said.

He crouched down beside her, so that their eyes were level.

“Is it always like that?” he asked.

She thought about it. “No. Sometimes it’s easy. Sometimes it’s worse.”

He looked at the baby, now wrapped in a quilt and still complaining. He looked back at her.

“I have watched you work before. At the camp. At the inn. I thought I knew what it was. I did not,” he said.

She didn’t know what to say to that. So she held out her good hand, the one with blood to the elbow, and he took it without hesitating and helped her to her feet. Outside, the sky over the wide water was turning grey. Chen Ye was sitting on the headman’s step with a sleeping child against each shoulder. He looked at the two of them in the doorway — at her hair, at the General’s sleeves, at their hands, which neither of them had yet remembered to let go — and said nothing whatever.

He didn’t need to. His face said it for him.

chapters.title: Two Things She Had Not Said
chapters.desc: By a fire on the ridge, she tells him who pushed her, and where she really comes from.
chapters.epigraph: “Everyone is a little frightened of me. You never were.”
chapters.content:
They left Wide Water at noon, after she had slept four hours on Old Nai’s floor and checked the baby twice and the headman’s hand once and the boy’s nail wound for the last time. Old Nai wouldn’t take silver. The General tried three times, and on the third she slapped his hand, quite hard, and said something to Shiyu that made Shiyu laugh until she had to hold her bad shoulder.

“What did she say?”

“That you have very nice manners for a scholar, and that if you try to pay her again she’ll feed you to the pike,” Shiyu said.

He bowed to Old Nai, very low, the way he would have bowed to a duchess. Old Nai looked deeply pleased with herself. In the end he left the silver with the headman, for the village, and nobody slapped him for that. The children walked them to the bottom of the hill path, and Little Ke cried, and Shiyu crouched down and promised in her terrible dialect that she would come back when the water was low and her arm was better. She meant it. She had already decided.

The path was steep and her legs were weaker than she wanted them to be. He didn’t offer to carry her. He walked beside her on the outside edge where the slope fell away, and when she stumbled, his hand was at her good elbow before she had finished stumbling, and when she was steady it went away again. Chen Ye and Tuo and the mules went on ahead and somehow always happened to stop and wait just when she needed to sit down.

They reached the shepherd’s hut on the ridge at dusk. Chen Ye made a fire outside it and cooked rice and dried fish in Tuo’s pot, and then announced that he and Tuo would sleep on the far side of the hut with the mules, because the mules liked company, and went there with a briskness that fooled nobody. The night was clear. Below them the hills fell away in folds of dark, and far off to the west there was a faint smudge of light that might have been the border post. Her father’s coat was around her shoulders. It smelled of his study — ink and dried herbs — and she kept turning her face into the collar.

They sat by the fire for a long time without talking. It was the kind of quiet they had always been good at.

Then she said, “I need to tell you something about the riverbank.”

He turned his head.

“I didn’t fall. I was pushed. I think you know that,” she said.

“I believed it. I could not prove it.” His voice was very even.

“Neither can I. But there’s a part you don’t know. Peng Yao was in front of me. Between me and the street. He stepped towards me, and I stepped back towards the river. His hands were in front of him the whole time. Open. Held out a little from his sides, like this — so I would see them. He wanted me to see them.” She held her good hand out to the fire. She showed him.

The General was completely still.

“The push came from behind. Low on my back. A flat hand. Hard,” she said.

It took him a moment. She watched it arrive.

“Then he did not do it alone.”

“No.”

“Someone was behind you.”

“Yes. I told myself afterwards that both the garrison soldiers had gone. I thought I saw them leave. But I was thinking about the child, not about them. I may have been wrong. There’s something else, but I don’t know what it’s worth. While I had the fever, I kept seeing a hand. The back of a man’s right hand, with an old burn scar across the knuckles. I think it was the soldier who carried the little boy from the bridge for me. I watched his hands when he lifted the boy, because I was worried about the neck. But I had a fever. I can swear to the push. I can swear to where Peng Yao’s hands were. I can’t swear to the scar.” She shook her head.

“You don’t need to swear to it. The garrison keeps a duty roll. Two soldiers went to the bridge. I will know both their names by tomorrow night, and whether either of them has a burned hand, and where he has been every hour since. And whether he has had any money he cannot explain.” He was looking into the fire, and his face had gone very quiet, in a way she had learned meant he was thinking at great speed.

“You’ll tell me what you find.”

He looked at her. “The moment I find it. I will not manage around you. I said so,” he said.

“I remember. Eleven words.” She almost smiled.

“You counted them.”

“I read them a great many times.”

He looked back at the fire. After a while he said, lower, “You said there was something you needed to tell me. You have told me one thing. You have the face you have when there is a second.”

She had known he would see it. Part of her had wanted him to. She pressed the pouch, where it hung at her sash again. Then she made herself take her hand away.

“At the capital, you told the Emperor you didn’t know where I learned to think the way I do,” she said.

He went still again. Not the way he had over Peng Yao. Differently.

“Chen Ye,” he said.

“Chen Ye, years ago. He thought I should know. You’ve never asked me. Not once. Not in the tent, not at the inn, not in any of the letters. I used to wonder why,” she agreed. She looked at the fire.

“Because I thought, that if I asked, you would have to choose between telling me and lying to me. And I did not think you would lie to me. So I did not want to make you choose,” he said slowly.

She had to look away for a moment. She said, “I’m going to tell you now. Because I don’t want there to be anything I haven’t told you. And because if I don’t say it tonight, out here, I don’t think I’ll ever find a better place. You can decide afterwards that I’m mad. I’ll understand.” She drew her father’s coat tighter.

“Tell me,” he said.

So she told him. She told him about a city he couldn’t imagine, where the streets were lit all night and the buildings were taller than the palace walls. About a hospital as big as the Northern Army’s whole camp, where she had been a surgeon — a physician who cut — for fifteen years, and had put people back together after carts and falls and fires and fights. About how good she had been at it, and how tired, and how alone. About driving home through rain after two days without sleep, and lights coming the wrong way out of the dark, and nothing after that.

And then waking up five years old, in a fever, in her mother’s arms in Qingzhou, with a whole other life behind her eyes and no idea how she had got there. She told it plainly, the way she would explain a diagnosis. She didn’t dress it up. She watched his face the whole time, and his face didn’t tell her anything at all, and she kept going anyway.

“I’ve never told anyone. Not my mother. Not my uncle. They know I’m strange. They decided a long time ago to love me without knowing why. That’s where I learned to think the way I do. I didn’t learn it. I brought it with me,” she said at the end.

The fire cracked. Somewhere on the far side of the hut, a mule shifted. He was quiet for so long that she began, despite everything, to be afraid.

Then he said, “Was it a good life?”

She stared at him. Of all the things she had imagined him saying — and she had imagined a great many, over four years, in the dark — she had never imagined that.

“It was a busy one. I was good at my work. I helped a lot of people. I was very lonely. I didn’t know how lonely until I came here and had a mother who fussed and a father who forgot to eat and an uncle who argued with me about everything,” she said, when she could. Her voice did something she didn’t intend.

He nodded slowly. “And when you went into the river. Did you think —” he said.

He stopped. She saw him understand it, all of it, before he had finished the sentence.

She said, “Yes, I thought: I died once, and woke up somewhere else. What if it happens again? What if I wake up there, and none of this is real, and I’m alone again with all the lights. And I thought, I don’t want to go back. Everything I want is here. And I held onto that branch.” She was crying now, and didn’t try to stop.

He reached out and took her good hand in both of his. His hands were warm from the fire.

“Then I am grateful to the branch,” he said.

It was so exactly the kind of thing he would say — so plain, so serious, so completely unlike anything anyone else in either of her lives would have said — that she laughed through the crying and couldn’t stop for a moment.

“You don’t think I’m mad.”

He said, “I have read every report you have written since you were sixteen. I told the Emperor I did not know where you learned to think like that. I have spent four years not knowing. It is a relief, a little, to know. It explains the first report.” He turned her hand over and looked at it, at the small calluses from the mortar and the brush.

“It explains the first report,” she repeated, and laughed again.

“And it explains why you were never frightened of me. I could not understand that. Everyone is a little frightened of me. You never were,” he said.

“I was frightened of you all the time. I just wasn’t frightened of what you might do to me,” she said.

He was quiet. Then: “I will not tell anyone.”

“I know.”

“Not the Emperor. Not Chen Ye.”

“Chen Ye will guess.”

“Chen Ye guesses everything. That is not the same as being told,” he said.

They sat for a long time after that with her hand in his, watching the fire burn down. At some point she fell asleep against his shoulder with her father’s coat around her. He didn’t move until morning. He told her later it was the best night’s sleep he hadn’t had in years.

chapters.title: The Second Bend at Dawn
chapters.desc: Home, her father on the riverbank, and a soldier with a burned hand.
chapters.epigraph: “Every patient. Every day. The same format. I didn’t miss one.” — Mei Yun, the morning Shiyu came home
chapters.content:
The moment they came down off the hill path onto the river plain, he stopped being a private scholar following a river. She watched it happen. One step he was walking beside her in a grey robe with mud to the knees. The next he had seen the flag of the border post, and something in his shoulders settled into place, and by the time they reached the post he was giving orders.

A rider to Qingzhou, now, on the fastest horse, to the governor’s residence: She is safe. She is with me. We will be home by morning. A second rider to the garrison commander: the duty roll for the day of the riverbank, the names of every soldier sent to the bridge at the second bend, and both of those men to be found and held, separately, before nightfall, without being told why. A carriage from the post, with as many quilts as could be found, because the physician had one working arm and wasn’t riding forty li on a horse.

“I can ride,” Shiyu said.

“I know you can. You are not going to,” he said.

She opened her mouth.

“Please,” he said.

She closed it again. He had never said please to her before. She got into the carriage.

Chen Ye didn’t get into the carriage. He took the second-best horse and a copy of the order to the garrison, and he looked at the General for a moment, and the General said, “The right hand. A burn across the knuckles,” and Chen Ye nodded once and was gone down the river road before the dust from the first rider had settled.

They travelled through the night. The carriage was hard and the road was bad, and she slept anyway, in snatches, with her head against the window frame and her father’s coat around her. Each time she woke, he was riding beside the window. Once she woke and he was looking in at her, and he didn’t look away when she caught him. He just went on looking, as if he had decided he was allowed to now.

They came into Qingzhou from the east, along the river path, as the sky was going from black to grey. She knew where they were before she saw it. The river had a different voice at the second bend — louder, harder, the water piling up against the rocks before the gorge. She had never in her life been afraid of that sound. Now her whole body went tight at it, and she was angry with herself, and she breathed through it the way she had taught a hundred frightened patients to breathe.

“Stop here,” she said through the window.

He didn’t ask why. He stopped the carriage. She climbed down carefully. The bank was wet with dew. Fifty paces ahead, at the very edge where the path ran beside the water, a man was standing alone with his back to them, looking at the river. He wasn’t young. His shoulders were rounded. He had a notebook in one hand. He didn’t have a coat on. It was cold, at dawn, by the river.

She walked towards him. Her legs weren’t steady and she didn’t care.

“Father,” she said.

He turned around. She had seen her father surprised many times. She had seen him surprised by plants, by old books, by a well-argued footnote. She had never seen his face do what it did now. It went loose and young and open, all at once, like a child’s, and the notebook fell out of his hand into the wet grass. He didn’t say anything. He took two steps and put his arms around her, very carefully, minding the sling, and held on.

“You weren’t wearing your coat. It’s cold. You’re freezing,” she said into his shoulder. Her voice had gone to pieces.

“I gave it away. To a young man going over a mountain. I knew you’d be cold,” her father said. He held her tighter.

Behind them, the General had stopped by the carriage and was standing very still, looking at the river. After a while her father let go, and wiped his face with his sleeve, and bent stiffly to pick up his notebook. He brushed the wet grass off it with great care. Then he turned to the General, and he didn’t bow, and he didn’t do any of the correct things a governor does when a supreme commander stands on his riverbank.

He just said, “Thank you.”

“She came back by herself. I only walked beside her,” the General said.

Yun Chengde looked at him for a moment, the slightly bewildered look he gave things that were more than he had expected.

“Yes. That’s what I meant,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was at the gate. The gate stood open. A lamp hung beside it, still lit in the grey light, and it had the look of a lamp that had been lit every night for a long time. Her mother stood under it in her house robe with her hair down, which Shiyu hadn’t seen since she was a small child. She didn’t run either. She waited until her daughter was close enough to touch, and then she put both hands on her face, one on each cheek, careful of the bruise, and looked at her for a long time.

“You’re thin,” her mother said.

“I know.”

“You’ll eat.”

“Yes, Mother.”

Her mother nodded. That settled everything. Then she put her forehead against her daughter’s forehead and stood like that, saying nothing, while the lamp burned beside them. When she finally stepped back, she looked past Shiyu to the General, who had stopped outside the gate.

“You’ll come in. You’ll eat too. You look worse than she does,” she said. It wasn’t a question.

He came in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mei Yun arrived at the residence an hour later, running, with her hair half pinned and a clinic apron still on. She stopped in the doorway of the room where Shiyu was sitting with a bowl of congee and her uncle prodding at her shoulder, and she looked at her for one breath with a completely naked face.

Then she burst into tears, loudly, like a child.

Then she stopped, wiped her face fiercely with the apron, and said, “I kept the records.”

“I know you did,” Shiyu said.

“Every patient. Every day. The same format. I didn’t miss one. Old Master Feng came every morning and asked. I told him you’d gone to the capital. He didn’t believe me. He brought pears anyway. There are a great many pears.” Her voice wobbled and she ignored it.

Shiyu put down the congee and held out her good arm, and Mei Yun crossed the room in three steps and hugged her so hard that Uncle Xiang said, “The shoulder, girl,” and was ignored by both of them.

Her uncle had ridden down from the camp the day the news reached him. He had spent the last ten days, according to her mother, being extremely rude to everyone. He examined the shoulder now with fingers that weren’t as steady as they should have been, and pronounced the reduction adequate, for a fishing village, and the sling disgraceful, and made her a new one himself. He didn’t say anything else for some time. When he had finished tying it, he put his hand on her head, briefly, the way he had when she was eight, and went out of the room rather fast.

She read Mei Yun’s records that afternoon, in bed, because her mother wouldn’t let her get up. They were very good. The handwriting was neater than her own. In the margin of the eighth day, next to a note about a child with a fever, Mei Yun had written in very small characters: She would have tried the willow bark first. I tried the willow bark first. Shiyu put her hand over the line and lay still for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Ye came to the residence at dusk. He found the General in the courtyard, where he had been since the afternoon — not sleeping, though her mother had told him twice to sleep, but sitting on the bench under the window of the room where Shiyu was resting. Chen Ye didn’t remark on this.

He said, “Duan Ping, garrison infantry, six years’ service. Right hand burned across the knuckles when he was a boy. He was one of the two soldiers sent to the bridge. He asked for leave the morning after the riverbank. He’s spent it in a gambling house in the river district, losing more silver than a soldier earns in a year.”

The General didn’t move.

Chen Ye said, “I had him brought to the garrison. I sat down across the table from him. I hadn’t said anything yet. He started talking before I’d finished sitting down. Peng Yao paid him. Peng Yao told him where to stand. He says he only meant to frighten her. He says he didn’t think the bank would give way.” Something cold crossed his face, very briefly.

“And the silver.”

“From a man who came to him in the river district a month ago. A steward, he says, from a great house in the capital. He knew the man’s face. I showed him some faces. It is the steward of Deputy Minister Qiao.” Chen Ye held out a folded paper.

The General took the paper. He didn’t open it. He knew the name. He had known it since the day she first told him where Peng Yao had come from.

“She knew. Didn’t she. About the hand,” Chen Ye said.

“She worked it out. On a stranger’s floor, with a fever. And then she told me she wasn’t sure,” the General said. He looked up at the window.

Chen Ye followed his gaze.

“Of course she did,” he said.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.desc: A dry old censor, a careful witness, and the General answering the word “irregular” in public.
chapters.epigraph: “If the Censorate needs a word for that, the word it is looking for is not impropriety.” — the General, in public
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
The Censorate sent a censor named Fang Mingshan, who arrived in Qingzhou eleven days later with two clerks, a chest of documents, and a reputation for having once made a provincial governor cry in open court. He was a small, dry, elderly man with very clean fingernails. He took the garrison’s administrative hall for the hearing, had the benches moved so that nobody could sit at the back, and announced that he would hear everything in one day, in order, and that anyone who wasted his time would be noted in the record as having wasted it.

Shiyu liked him at once. Her shoulder was out of the sling by then, though not yet strong. She wore a plain dark jacket — not the green coat, which had been the presentation coat, and this wasn’t that kind of day — and she sat on the witness bench with her hands folded in her lap and her mother’s voice in her head: Eat. Sleep. Tell the truth. Don’t let them hurry you.

The General sat on the other side of the hall, among the officials, in full uniform for the first time since she had seen him on the riverbank road. He hadn’t come near her that morning. He had told her he wouldn’t, the night before, so that nobody could say afterwards that he had spoken to her before she gave her evidence. She had told him that was very sensible and she hated it.

Peng Yao was brought in under guard. She hadn’t seen him since the riverbank. He looked smaller. His robe was good and clean, and someone had let him shave, and he had put the pleasant expression back on, though it no longer fitted quite right. He bowed to the censor correctly. He didn’t look at her. Duan Ping was brought in after him, and he looked at no one at all.

The censor took the riverbank first. The river worker who had raised the alarm said what he had seen from the far end of the path: a woman in the water, and a man in a garrison coat walking away up the slope very fast, not running. He had thought the man was going for help. The man hadn’t come back. The garrison commander read out the duty roll. Two soldiers sent to the bridge. One had returned to the garrison within the hour. One hadn’t returned until the following morning, and had asked for leave.

Duan Ping’s confession was read into the record by a clerk, slowly, every word. The silver. The instructions. Where to stand. He said she would step back. He said all I had to do was be there when she did. Duan Ping sat with his burned hand in his lap and his head down and didn’t deny any of it. Once, when the clerk read out I only meant to frighten her, his shoulders shook.

Then the censor called her. She stood. She walked to the front of the hall. She told it the way she had told it to the General by the fire: in order, without colour, exactly as much as she knew and no more. The child at the bridge. The two soldiers. Peng Yao at the corner of the path. What he said. Where he stood. Where his hands were.

“And the push,” said the censor.

“From behind. Low on the back. A flat hand,” she said.

“Did you see whose hand it was?”

“No.”

A small movement on the far side of the hall. Peng Yao had lifted his head.

“You did not see,” the censor said.

“I did not see. I was facing Peng Yao. Afterwards, in a fever, I remembered a burn scar on the back of a man’s hand. I told the General at the time that I couldn’t swear to it, because I had a fever when I remembered it. I still can’t swear to it. I can swear to the push. I can swear that Peng Yao was in front of me the whole time, and that both his hands were in front of him, open, where I could see them.” She kept her eyes on the censor.

“The physician admits that she does not know who touched her,” said Peng Yao, in his pleasant voice.

The censor turned his head very slowly and looked at him, and Peng Yao stopped.

“You will have your turn. It is not now. Why do you mention his hands? A man may stand with his hands wherever he likes,” the censor said. He looked back at Shiyu.

She said, “He wanted me to see them. That’s why I remember them. He held them out a little from his sides, like a man showing you he isn’t carrying anything. I’ve stood across from a great many frightened people, and a great many people who were lying to me. People don’t stand like that by accident. He was making sure that whatever happened next, I would remember that it wasn’t his hands. I did remember. It’s why I knew there was someone behind me.” She showed the censor, exactly as she had shown the General.

The hall was very quiet. The censor wrote something down. It took him a long time. When it was Peng Yao’s turn, he did well, for a while. He was calm and reasonable and regretful. He had gone to the riverbank to give the physician advice. He had nothing to do with any soldier. Duan Ping was a gambler and a liar who had pushed a woman into a river for reasons of his own, and was now trying to save his neck by blaming a man of good family. It was a tragedy. He was very sorry for it.

Then the censor asked him, mildly, how a garrison infantryman on a soldier’s pay had come to be carrying silver stamped with the mark of the capital’s Western Mint. Peng Yao said he had no idea. The censor asked him how he explained that a steward of Deputy Minister Qiao’s household had been seen in the river district of Qingzhou on three separate days in the month before the riverbank, and had stayed at the same lodging house as Peng Yao.

Peng Yao said that Qingzhou was a large city. The censor asked him why, on the morning after the riverbank, he had written a letter to Deputy Minister Qiao — a copy of which the courier station had kept, as courier stations do — containing the sentence The difficulty in Qingzhou has resolved itself. Peng Yao didn’t answer that. The pleasant expression didn’t so much fall off his face as slowly stop being there. What was left underneath it wasn’t frightening. It was only tired, and bitter, and very ordinary.

✦ ✦ ✦

The General was called last. He stood up in his uniform, and every official in the hall sat a little straighter, and he walked to the front and faced the censor and didn’t look at her once. He spoke briefly about the inquiry he had already held, and the records he had already sent to the Emperor. He spoke about Peng Yao’s first report, and the attempt to stop the direct letters, and the concern sent to the Censorate. He did it in the flat, plain voice he used for battle reports, and it was devastating, because it was so obviously not trying to be.

Then the censor said, “The concern that Peng Yao submitted to this office described your correspondence with the physician as an irregularity. You have said you wished to respond to that formally.”

“Yes,” said the General.

Shiyu’s hands tightened in her lap.

He said, “There is nothing irregular about it. I wrote to the physician every two weeks for most of a year. Some of the letters were about the commission. Some of them were not. I wrote them because I wanted to write to her. She answered them, I believe, for the same reason. If the Censorate needs a word for that, the word it is looking for is not impropriety.” He paused, and for the first time his voice wasn’t quite flat.

Nobody in the hall moved. The censor looked at him over his clean fingernails for a long moment. Then he looked across the hall at Shiyu.

“Physician. Do you wish to add anything?” he said.

She stood up. Her knees weren’t entirely reliable. She didn’t care.

“Only that he’s right. I answered them for the same reason,” she said.

She sat down again. On the far side of the hall, Chen Ye looked at the ceiling with the face of a man trying very hard not to look at anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The censor gave his findings at sunset. Duan Ping: to be sent to the Ministry of Justice for sentence, with a note that he had confessed fully and without being pressed, and that the physician he had injured had asked, in writing, that his sentence take account of the fact that he had a mother in the river district who depended on him. Shiyu had written the note that morning. She wasn’t sure, even now, whether she had done it because it was right or because she wanted to be the kind of person who did it. She thought perhaps those weren’t so different.

Peng Yao: to be stripped of his rank and post, and sent to the Ministry of Justice for the attempted murder of an imperial appointee. The censor recommended exile to the far southern frontier, for life. Deputy Minister Qiao: a report to be sent to the Emperor, with every document attached.

That night, very late, the General came to the clinic. She was in the preparation room, because she couldn’t sleep and her hands wanted something to do. He sat down on the stool beside her without being asked.

“The Emperor’s reply about Qiao will take a week. He will be dismissed. He will be allowed to say it is for his health,” he said.

“That seems generous.”

“It is the kind of generous that leaves no complications. There is one more thing. The Emperor gave me permission, some weeks ago, to answer for this personally. I have decided how.” He watched her grind dried mugwort for a while.

She put the pestle down and looked at him.

He said, “There will be a fence at the second bend. Stone posts and a timber rail, the whole length of the path, and along the bridge abutment where the children jump. The city has been meaning to build it for as long as anyone can remember. It will be built this autumn. At the end of it there will be a stone saying who paid for it. Deputy Minister Qiao is going to pay for it. Out of his own household. I have already written to him to explain that he would like to.”

She stared at him. “The stone. It will say his name,” she said slowly.

“In large characters. Very clearly cut. Where every child who sits on that fence will be able to read it,” he said.

“That’s petty,” she said.

“Yes,” he agreed.

She started to laugh. She couldn’t help it. She laughed until her shoulder ached and she had to hold it, and he sat on the stool beside her and watched her laugh with an expression she had never seen on his face before. It took her a moment to realise what it was. He was pleased with himself.

chapters.title: Something for Himself
chapters.desc: For the first time in his life, he asks for something that isn’t for the army.
chapters.epigraph: “I will be bad at it. You will have to tell me when I am being bad at it.”
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
He was meant to go north at the end of the ninth month. He had been away from the camp for six weeks. There were dispatches arriving every day. Wei Tiecheng had written twice, in his short blunt hand: the first letter said Everything is in order, and the second said Everything is still in order, come back anyway, which from Wei Tiecheng was very nearly a plea. She knew all of this. She knew he couldn’t stay. She had known from the beginning, from the first letter, that this was what it would always be: a season of him, and then the road north, and then letters. She had told herself she could live with that. She thought she probably could.

On the morning before he was due to leave, he came to the clinic at midday, when the waiting room was empty and Mei Yun had gone to the market, and found her in the preparation room with the mortar. He pulled the second stool from the wall and sat down beside her, the way he had on his first morning in Qingzhou, a lifetime ago at the start of the summer. He didn’t say anything for a while. She ground the herbs. He watched.

Then he said, “I have never asked anyone for anything.”

She stopped.

He said, “I have asked for things for the army. Men. Grain. Horses. Authority. I have asked the Emperor for a great many things, and all of them were for the army. When I was fifteen, after my parents died, he asked me what I wanted. I didn’t understand the question. I said I wanted to be useful. He gave me a sword and a tutor and sent me north. I have been useful ever since.” He was looking at the herb cabinet, not at her.

She set the pestle down without a sound.

He said, “Chen Ye says I don’t know how to want things for myself. He is usually right about me. He was right about this. I am trying to learn. I am not very good at it. So I am going to say this plainly, because I don’t know any other way to say it.” He turned his head and looked at her then.

She waited. She had always known how to wait for him.

“I want to marry you. If you will have me,” he said.

The preparation room was very quiet. Outside, in the lane, someone was calling out the price of chestnuts. She found that she had known he would say it — had known for weeks, perhaps since the fire on the ridge — and that knowing made no difference at all. It still went through her like the first warm day of spring.

He said, “Before you answer. I have thought about the rest of it. I don’t want you to say yes and then find out what you have said yes to.”

“Tell me,” she said.

He told her. He had written to the Emperor asking to divide the year. Winter on the frontier, when the passes closed and the fighting stopped and the army sat in its winter quarters; that was when the camp most needed a physician who could teach. The rest of the year in Qingzhou, with the southern garrison under his command and the frontier under Wei Tiecheng, who had been asking for it for two years and would hold it better than anyone. Lin Wenyuan had already drawn up the dispatch routes. Lü Yue had read the plan and said it was sound, which from Lü Yue was the same as a blessing.

“And the clinic. When you are in the north, Mei Yun runs it. If you think she is ready,” he said.

“She’s ready. She’s been ready for a year. I just hadn’t told her,” Shiyu said.

He said, “And when you are here, you work. As you work now. As much as you want. I would not know how to stop you. I would not want to be the kind of man who tried.”

She looked at him for a long moment. “You’ve thought about this for a while,” she said.

“Since the inn. Before the inn, if I am honest. I did not let myself think it in words until the capital.”

“And the Emperor said yes? To dividing the year?”

“The Emperor has not answered yet. I did not want to ask him for the rest of it until I had asked you.” Something moved at the corner of his mouth.

She laughed — a short, shaky sound — and then stopped laughing, because she was going to cry if she didn’t, and she had cried enough this month.

“I have conditions,” she said.

He nodded at once, as though he had expected nothing else. “Tell me.”

“I keep my name on my work. Always. Not your name. Mine.”

“Yes.”

“The camp gets a proper medical tent. Not a tent — a building. With a floor. And real lamps. Not fish-oil.”

The corner of his mouth moved again. “Yes.”

“I go back to Wide Water when the water is low. Every year, if I can. Old Nai is going to need her knees looked at, and I promised Little Ke.”

“I will come with you. I owe a man a great deal of silver for a hill path,” he said.

“And — And you have to tell me. When something is wrong. When you’re hurt, or afraid, or tired, or you don’t know what to do. You can’t keep it all behind your face for me. I’ve spent four years learning to read what you don’t say. I don’t want to have to spend the rest of my life doing it.” She stopped. This one was harder. She made herself say it anyway, because she had decided four years ago in a tent that she would always tell him the truth.

He was quiet for a long time. “That one is difficult,” he said at last.

“I know.”

“I will try. I will be bad at it. You will have to tell me when I am being bad at it,” he said.

“I will. Often,” she said.

“Then yes. To all of it,” he said.

She looked down at the mortar, and the herbs half ground in it, and her own hands, which had been steady through a gorge and a fever and a breech birth by fish-oil light, and weren’t steady now.

“Then yes. I’ll marry you,” she said.

He didn’t move for a moment. She thought perhaps he hadn’t quite believed she would say it, even now, even after everything.

Then he reached out and took her face in his two hands, very carefully, the way a man holds something he has been told is fragile and knows isn’t, and he kissed her. It wasn’t a long kiss. He wasn’t a man who did anything for longer than it needed. But it wasn’t careful, either, after the first moment, and when it ended she found that she was holding onto the front of his coat with both hands, the bad shoulder included, and that she didn’t remember deciding to.

He rested his forehead against hers.

“You have herbs on your fingers,” he said.

“I was working.”

“I know. I have always liked watching you work.” His voice had gone very low.

The front door of the clinic opened and closed. There was a clatter of baskets and Mei Yun’s voice calling, “The chestnut man was robbing everyone, so I got pears instead, there are —”

She came into the preparation room doorway and stopped. She looked at the two of them — at Shiyu’s hands on his coat, at his hands on Shiyu’s face, at the mortar forgotten on the table — and her own face did something complicated and then went perfectly, serenely blank.

“I’ll be in the front. Sorting pears. For some time,” she said.

She went. From the front room, a moment later, very faintly, came the sound of someone trying not to make a sound and failing. Shiyu put her face against his shoulder and laughed until she couldn’t breathe.

chapters.title: A Very Formal Letter
chapters.desc: Her father asks one question. The Emperor reads a letter twice and smiles.
chapters.epigraph: “I fell in love with her watching her work, sir. It would be a strange thing to marry her and ask her to stop.” — the General, to her father
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
He didn’t go north the next morning. He sent a dispatch to Wei Tiecheng instead, which Chen Ye carried to the garrison, and which Chen Ye told Shiyu afterwards had contained only one line: One more month. Then I bring you a physician for the winter. You will understand. Wei Tiecheng’s answer came back by relay rider four days later, and it was even shorter. It said: Finally.

That afternoon he went to see her father.

There were correct ways to do this. Shiyu knew them, and so did he. A matchmaker should go first, with gifts and the eight characters of his birth, and the families should consult an almanac, and nobody should say anything directly to anybody for at least a month. Her mother had explained all of this to her at breakfast with great seriousness, and then said he wouldn’t do any of that, would he.

“No, Mother,” Shiyu had said.

Her mother had sighed. “Good. I never liked the Wang family’s matchmaker anyway.”

He went to her father’s study alone, in the plain dark coat he wore in Qingzhou, carrying nothing. Shiyu wasn’t in the room. She was in the courtyard outside it, sitting on the edge of the herb bed with a book open in her lap that she wasn’t reading. Her mother was in the corridor on the other side of the study door, arranging and rearranging a vase of chrysanthemums that hadn’t needed arranging the first time.

Through the window, Shiyu could see her father at his desk, surrounded by the Tang companion texts, with his nose two finger-widths from the page, the way he always read. He looked up when the General came in and blinked several times. Then he took off his outer robe, which he only did for people he considered family, and put it over the back of his chair.

She couldn’t hear most of what they said. She heard the General’s voice, low and even, for some time. She heard her father say, “Ah,” once, and then that yes, he had wondered, and then, after a long pause, a question.

She heard the question. Everyone in the house heard it. Her father had a scholar’s voice, made for reading aloud in large halls, and when he was serious he forgot to lower it.

“Will you let her work?”

There was a silence. Then the General’s answer, quieter, but not so quiet that it didn’t carry through a paper window:

“I could not stop her if I tried. I would not want to be the kind of man who tried. I fell in love with her watching her work, sir. It would be a strange thing to marry her and ask her to stop.”

Shiyu closed the book in her lap. She sat very still in the autumn sun.

In the study, her father was quiet for a long time. Then he said, in his ordinary voice, the slightly vague one, “Good. Good. That was the only thing, really. She’s been working since she was five, you know. Even before that she was — Well. She was always herself. I never understood her, entirely. I hope you don’t expect to.”

“No, sir.”

“Good. Her mother will say yes before I do. She’s been standing outside that door for a quarter of an hour.” A rustle of paper.

The study door opened. Her mother came in holding the vase of chrysanthemums, as if she had simply happened to be passing with it, and set it down on the desk on top of the Tang companion texts, which made her father make a small anguished noise.

“Yes,” her mother said.

“I hadn’t asked you yet,” said the General.

“I know. I’m saving you the trouble. You’ll eat with us tonight. And every night you’re in Qingzhou. I won’t have you eating alone,” said her mother. She looked at him.

Something happened to the General’s face that Shiyu, watching through the window, had to look away from, because it seemed too private to watch.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wrote the letter to the Emperor that night, at the writing table in the governor’s guest room. He wrote it four times. The first three he burned in the brazier. He told her afterwards that the first had been too short, the second too long, and the third had sounded like a request for winter supplies. The fourth he wrote slowly, in his most careful formal hand, with all the correct phrases a nephew uses when he petitions the throne. He asked for the division of the year, as he had already explained. Then he asked for the other thing.

He didn’t revise it. He sealed it with his own seal and gave it to the relay rider before dawn.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Emperor received it six days later, in the small study behind the audience hall where he read the dispatches that mattered. It was raining in the capital. He had a cold. He had spent the morning listening to the Ministry of Rites argue about the order of precedence at the winter sacrifice, and he had spent the afternoon reading Deputy Minister Qiao’s letter of resignation, which was very long and full of references to his health. He wasn’t in a good temper.

His secretary laid the letter from Qingzhou on top of the pile without being told to. The Emperor broke the seal. He read the first part, about dividing the year between the frontier and the south, and nodded slowly. It was sound. He had expected it. He would approve it.

Then he read the second part. He read it again. His secretary, who had served him for twenty-two years and had seen him receive news of victories and plagues and the deaths of three of his brothers, would say afterwards that he had never seen what happened next. The Emperor set the letter down on the desk. He sat back in his chair. And he smiled — not the thin, careful smile he gave ministers, but something broad and sudden that took ten years off his face.

“Well, it took him long enough,” he said, to nobody.

He picked up his brush. His reply reached Qingzhou eight days later, carried by an imperial messenger in full ceremonial dress, who had to ask three people in the river district for directions to the governor’s residence and was given four different answers. The decree was correct in every way. It granted the division of the year. It granted the marriage, in the long formal language of the throne, with the names and titles of both parties written out in full. It named the physician Yun Shiyu a Lady of the Fourth Rank in her own right, for service to the Northern Army and to the people of Qingzhou, so that nobody would ever be able to say she had been given a title only because of whom she married.

At the bottom, below the imperial seal, in the Emperor’s own hand, there was one more line. It wasn’t in the language of the throne.

Bring her to dinner at the new year. I want to ask her about page seven.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two nights before the wedding, he gave her mother something. Shiyu didn’t see it happen. Her mother told her about it later, much later, on the morning of the wedding. He had come to find Lady Ren in the courtyard, where she was taking in the lamp from the gate — she still lit it every night, though there was no longer any reason, because she said she had got used to it. He had held out his hand, and in it was a small jade hairpin carved with clouds.

He said, “A fishing family found it. Below the gorge. I have been carrying it. I thought you should be the one to give it back to her.”

Her mother had taken it, and looked at it for a long time in the light from the lamp.

“You could have given it to her yourself. Weeks ago,” she said.

“Yes, I wanted you to have the chance to put it in her hair again,” he said.

Her mother said she hadn’t been able to say anything to that. She had only nodded, and closed her hand around the hairpin, and gone inside. And she had put it away in her own jewel box, in the drawer where she kept the things that mattered, to wait.

chapters.title: The Wedding
chapters.desc: A camphorwood box, a jade hairpin, and two names said for the first time.
chapters.epigraph: “Take as long as you like, Chief Physician. I’ll still be here.” — the General, to her uncle, at the bowing
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
They were married in Qingzhou in the tenth month, when the chrysanthemums were out along every wall in the city and the river had gone back to its ordinary autumn brown. The Five arrived three days before, which Shiyu hadn’t expected, since someone had to be holding the frontier. It turned out that Wei Tiecheng had left it with his second-in-command and a long list of instructions, and had announced to the whole camp that anyone who sent him a dispatch during the wedding would be digging latrines until spring. Lin Wenyuan had drawn up the duty rosters for the journey. Zhou Hua had complained about the length of the journey every day of it. Lü Yue had said nothing at all, the whole way, which Chen Ye said meant he was very moved.

They came to the clinic on the first afternoon, all five of them, in plain clothes, and stood in her front room looking at the shelves.

“So this is where it all comes from,” said Zhou Hua, with great satisfaction, and immediately knocked over a jar of dried chrysanthemum.

Wei Tiecheng had brought her a box. He held it out without looking at her, the way he had once stood in the entrance of her medical tent with his arms crossed, preparing to say something he didn’t want to say. It was a medicine case, made of dark camphorwood, with twelve small drawers that fitted perfectly and a brass catch shaped like a cloud. The joints were so fine she couldn’t see them.

“Who made this?” she said.

Wei Tiecheng looked at the ceiling.

Zhou Hua said, “He did. All summer. In the evenings. He wouldn’t let anyone see it. He cut his thumb on the third drawer and wouldn’t let anyone look at that either.”

“For the salt water. The twelve men from my unit. I said I had noted it. I wanted — I wanted it noted properly,” Wei Tiecheng said gruffly. He stopped. His scarred face had gone a dull red.

She held the box in both hands. She didn’t trust herself to say anything long.

“It’s been noted. Thank you,” she said.

He nodded once, sharply, and went to look very hard at the herb cabinet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of the wedding, her mother put the jade hairpin in her hair.

She did it in the same room where she had done it before the capital, with the same small, quick movements. She didn’t say anything while she did it. When it was done, she stepped back and looked at her daughter in the red wedding robe, and her eyes filled, and she said, “There,” in a voice that wasn’t steady at all.

“Mother. Where did you —” Shiyu said.

Her mother told her. About the courtyard, and the lamp, and what he had said. Shiyu sat very still for a while after that, and her mother held her hand, and neither of them said anything, and it was one of the best moments of the whole day.

✦ ✦ ✦

The red veil meant she saw very little of the ceremony itself. She saw her own feet, and the hem of her robe, and the floor of her father’s great hall. She heard a great deal. She heard her father reading out the blessing in his large-hall scholar’s voice, and losing his place once, and finding it again. She heard Old Master Feng in the front row telling everyone around him that he had known from the very beginning, from the first day he heard two voices in the consultation room. She heard Mei Yun sniffing loudly and Chen Ye, beside her, under his breath handing her a handkerchief.

She heard her uncle, at the moment when the families bowed to each other, say in a low voice to the General, “I’m still deciding whether to be angry with you.”

And the General’s answer, just as low: “Take as long as you like, Chief Physician. I’ll still be here.”

Then a hand lifted the veil. The hall was bright after the red dark. There were a great many faces. She didn’t look at any of them. She looked at him, standing in front of her in red, with the veil in his hand. His face wasn’t managing anything at all. It hadn’t been managing anything, she realised, since the street in Wide Water. He had simply stopped.

He looked at her for a long moment, in front of everyone.

“Finally,” he said, under his breath.

As if she had been somewhere he couldn’t see, and had come back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The feast went on for most of the afternoon and well into the evening, and was louder than any occasion the governor’s residence had held in a hundred years. Zhou Hua danced, badly, on his healed leg, and insisted it was a northern dance, and Wei Tiecheng told everyone it wasn’t. Her father showed the Tang companion texts to Lin Wenyuan, who turned out to have read them, and the two of them disappeared into a corner and weren’t seen again for an hour. Tuo the salt trader had come all the way over the hill path with his two mules, uninvited, carrying a sack of salt as a wedding gift and a message from Old Nai, which Shiyu translated with some care and the guests decided was a blessing. It wasn’t, entirely. Old Nai had said that if the scholar didn’t treat her well, she would come down the river herself.

Lin Wenyuan had written the wedding couplets. They hung on either side of the hall door in his precise, beautiful hand, and everyone who came in stopped to read them.

The cloud that came down with the rain stayed to heal the city.
The cloud that rose with the battle came back to stand beside her.

Shiyu read them twice on her way into the feast. She found Lin Wenyuan afterwards, and thanked him, and he looked down at his ink-stained fingers and said, “I have been writing that one in my head since the inn. It seemed a waste not to use it.”

Late in the evening, Lü Yue came to find her. He was the oldest of the Five, and the most serious, and he had never once in four years said anything to her that wasn’t strictly necessary. He stood in front of her now in his good grey robe, and for a moment she thought he was going to say nothing at all. Then he bowed — not the bow a man gives a general’s new wife, but the slow, full bow a junior physician gives a senior one.

He said, “The logic was sound. The first time you explained it to me, in the tent. I have thought so ever since. He chose well. So did you.” He straightened.

He went away before she could answer. She stood there for some time afterwards, holding her cup, and found that it was very hard to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

Near the end of the night, she went out into the courtyard for some air and found Chen Ye there, leaning against the wall by the gate, watching the lanterns. Mei Yun was there too, sitting on the edge of the herb bed. The two of them weren’t talking. They had the look of two people who had just finished talking about something and hadn’t yet decided what they thought about it.

Shiyu stopped in the doorway. Neither of them had seen her.

“Are you going to say your one true thing now, and then leave?” Mei Yun said.

Chen Ye considered this.

“Not tonight. I thought I might stay,” he said.

Mei Yun looked at him for a long moment. Then she moved over on the edge of the herb bed, very slightly. Not enough to mean anything. Exactly enough to mean something. He sat down. Shiyu went back inside without a sound and didn’t tell anyone what she had seen. She thought Mei Yun would tell her eventually, probably at great length.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, when the guests had finally gone and the lanterns were burning low and the house had gone quiet, they sat together on the edge of the bed in the room her mother had prepared, still in their wedding red, and for a while neither of them said anything. It was a good silence. It was one of theirs.

“You never say my name,” she said at last.

He turned his head.

She said, “In four years. You’ve called me Physician and you’ve called me nothing at all. You said it once, in the capital, when I was walking away. Shiyu. Just once. I’ve thought about it more than I want to admit.”

He was quiet for a moment. “I did not think I had the right. Before,” he said.

“And now?”

He looked at her in the low lamplight — the hairpin, the red robe, the bruise on her cheekbone long since gone.

“Shiyu,” he said.

It was very quiet. It was the way he said everything that mattered: flat and certain, as if it were simply a fact. She found she had to take a breath before she could answer. And then she said the thing she had never said either, not once, not in four years of letters and tents and inns and riverbanks — the name nobody had called him since he was fifteen, except the Emperor.

“Lingyun,” she said.

She felt it land. She watched it go all the way through him. He closed his eyes. When he opened them again, he didn’t say anything at all. He didn’t need to. For once in his life, everything he felt was in his face, and he let her see all of it, and didn’t look away.

chapters.title: The Song of Clouds
chapters.desc: Two years later, she watches the army ride in from the same balcony. This time he looks up.
chapters.epigraph: “It isn’t for you. It’s for the people who watched.” — Mei Yun, on the Song of Clouds
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
Two years later, in the spring, the Northern Army came back through Qingzhou on its way south from the winter quarters, and Yun Shiyu went up to the balcony of her father’s house to watch it pass. She didn’t need to. She had come down from the frontier herself three weeks earlier, ahead of the army, the way she did every spring now, to open the clinic for the season and read Mei Yun’s winter records — which were, as always, better kept than her own. She knew exactly when the procession would arrive, and which road it would take, and who would be riding at the front of it. She could have waited for him at the gate like a sensible woman.

She went up to the balcony anyway. She liked it there. It was where it had started. The spring rains had stopped two days ago, and the city smelled of wet stone and herbs. Below her, the street was filling up the way it always did when the army came through: shopkeepers in their doorways, children on the walls, old women with stools, Old Master Feng at his corner with a basket of loquats he would certainly try to give her later. Further off, towards the river, she could see the long grey line of the fence along the second bend, with a row of small figures sitting on it, kicking their heels.

At the end of the fence there was a stone, as promised, very clearly cut. In two years the children of the river district had worn the characters smooth climbing on it. Deputy Minister Qiao, she had heard, had retired to the country for his health and didn’t visit the south. A great deal had happened in two years, and most of it had been work. The northern camp had a medical hall now. Not a tent — a building, with a timber floor that could be scrubbed and windows that faced south and lamps that burned good oil, not fish oil. She had insisted on the lamps. Wei Tiecheng had built the shelves himself, in the evenings, and had cut his thumb again, and had again refused to let anyone look at it. Over two winters she had taught eleven army physicians to clean a wound with boiled salt water and to write down what happened afterwards, and three of them had already started arguing with her about method, which Uncle Xiang said was the surest sign they had been listening.

At the first new year, she had gone to dinner at the palace, as instructed. The Emperor had asked her about page seven for most of the first course and the whole of the second. At the end of the meal he had asked whether she would spend one month a year teaching at the Imperial Medical Academy. She had said yes, on condition that she could bring her own records and her own assistant, and that nobody would call her the Fairy Physician. The Emperor had agreed to the first two.

Every autumn, when the river dropped, she went back over the hill path to Wide Water. Old Nai’s knees were bad and getting worse, and Old Nai complained about them with enormous satisfaction to anyone who would listen. The headman’s granddaughter was walking. Little Ke, who was eight now, had announced that she was going to be a river doctor too, and followed Shiyu from house to house with a notebook made of trader’s paper, writing down everything in characters nobody else could read. The General came with her every time. He paid Tuo a great deal too much for the use of his mules, and Tuo laughed his dropped-pot laugh and took it.

And he was learning. He was bad at it, as he had said he would be. But in the second winter, when a patrol was caught in the passes by a snowstorm and didn’t come back for three days, he had come to the medical hall at midnight and stood in the doorway, and when she looked up he had said, quite plainly, “I can’t sleep. I’m afraid for them.” She had put down her brush and sat with him until the dawn, and the patrol had come in on the fourth morning, frostbitten and alive. Afterwards he had said, a little stiffly, that it had helped to say it. She had told him she knew. She hadn’t told him that it was the best thing he had ever said to her, because he would have been unbearable about it.

The clinic had changed too. There was a second sign over the door of the Qingcloud Medical Hall now, beside the old one, with Mei Yun’s name on it as physician of record. Mei Yun had wanted it smaller. Shiyu had made it exactly the same size and refused to discuss it. In the winters Mei Yun ran the Hall alone and was, by every account, terrifying. She was also, since the new year, betrothed to a certain personal guard, who had asked her in the courtyard of the governor’s residence and then — as he told the General afterwards, with great dignity — had stayed.

And there was a song. Shiyu hadn’t known about it until the first autumn after the wedding, when she heard it from the children in the river district and asked Mei Yun what it was. Mei Yun had been delighted to explain. It was a skipping song, the kind children make up out of whatever is in the air that year. It was about two clouds. One came down with the rain and stayed to heal the city; one rose with the battle and came back to stand beside her; and in the last verse the two clouds met over the river, and the river stopped being afraid. It didn’t rhyme very well. It had at least six endings, depending on which street you were in. The children sang it on the fence and in the lanes and outside the clinic door when they thought she could hear.

They called it the Song of Clouds. Shiyu found it excessive. She had said so, once, to Mei Yun, who had replied serenely that she wasn’t supposed to like it. It was for the people who had watched, not for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard the procession before she saw it — the hooves, the harness, a crowd going quiet and then loud again. The first riders came round the corner below the balcony, and behind them, on a black horse, in black armour with silver at the edges and his helmet carried at his side, came the Supreme Commander of the Northern Army. He looked older than he had at twenty-five, the first time she saw him from this railing. There were two grey hairs at his temple that she had found in the winter and refused to pull out. And he looked less cold. People in the crowd who had seen him come through before said so to each other; she heard them. He looks different. He looks — and then they didn’t quite have the word, and she didn’t supply it for them.

Her father’s household came out of the gate to greet him, the way it always did. Her father was in front, with ink on his sleeve and the first printed copy of his herb survey under his arm, which he had been carrying everywhere for a week. Her mother was beside him. Her uncle, down from the frontier with the army, was riding three horses back and already arguing with Lin Wenyuan about something.

The General turned his head to receive the greeting. And then, before he had finished nodding to her father, he looked up. He looked straight up at the balcony, at her — the way he hadn’t looked the first time, because the first time he hadn’t known she was there. He knew now. He always knew where she was in a room. He had told her once that it was the first thing he did, entering any room: find the door, find the danger, find her.

His face didn’t do anything that anyone else in that street would have noticed. But she had spent six years learning it. She saw the corner of his mouth, and she saw his eyes, and she knew exactly what they said. She pressed the back of her hand to her cheek. Warm. Yes.

“Purely academic,” she said to no one.

Then her other hand went, without her deciding, to the cloud-embroidered pouch at her sash, and pressed. Down in the street, he saw it. She watched him see it. She watched him understand that she was pressing it here, now, with nothing wrong anywhere in the world — and what that had to mean. That there was something she didn’t yet know how to say. He said something to her father. Her father looked up at the balcony, startled, and then waved, delighted, with the ink-stained sleeve. And the General handed his reins to Chen Ye, who took them without any expression whatsoever, and walked in through the gate.

She heard him on the stairs. He had never in his life taken stairs two at a time. He did now. He came out onto the balcony and stopped a pace from her. He was still in his armour. He smelled of horses and road dust and the north.

“You have something to tell me,” he said.

“How do you know?”

He looked at her hand, which was still on the pouch. She laughed, and let go of it. Her eyes had filled. She didn’t mind.

“I didn’t know how to put it in a letter. I wanted to see your face,” she said.

“Then tell me. I am looking at you,” he said.

So she told him.

She said, “Uncle Xiang is retiring at the end of the year. He wrote to the Emperor before he wrote to me. The Emperor wrote back with one name for his post. Chief Physician of the Northern Army. In my own name, not as anybody’s niece or anybody’s consultant. By the first snow it will be official. Nobody will ever be able to send me home in a supply carriage again.” She held his eyes.

She saw it land, the way she had seen everything land in him for six years — the half-breath, the stillness, and then the slow change all the way through. Except that this time he didn’t hold any of it back. He didn’t even try. He put his hands on either side of her face, armour and all, there on the balcony in full view of half of Qingzhou, and looked at her as if she were the first warm day after a very long winter.

Down in the street, the crowd had gone completely silent. Then, from somewhere near the river, faint and badly in tune, a row of children on a stone fence began, with great enthusiasm, to sing.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, when the house was quiet, she went to the chest at the foot of her old bed and took out a notebook she hadn’t opened in years. It was the one she had carried on the road south from the camp when she was sixteen, with her bundle and her uncle’s parting advice and a feeling in her chest she had no name for. Most of it was notes on patients. On the second evening of that journey, she had written one line about the General. Just one.

She found the page. The characters were small and careful, a girl’s hand trying very hard to be steady.

It was worth having done.

He came in while she was still looking at it, and sat down on the end of the bed beside her, and read it over her shoulder. She felt him go still. He knew those words. They were his. He had said them to her in the command tent at dawn, when she was sixteen and had just taken out his stitches and told him the work had been worth doing — and he had corrected her, very deliberately, by a few words. She had carried the correction home and written it down and never told him.

“You wrote that. On the way home,” he said.

“On the second evening. I thought it was the end of the story. I thought I was being very grown up about it,” she said.

He was quiet for a moment. Then he held out his hand, and she understood, and gave him the brush from the writing box. He wrote beneath her line, in the compressed, careful hand she had first seen in the margins of her reports — the hand she had waited for every two weeks, at the window, in the good light.

It still is.

He gave her back the brush. She looked at the two lines together for a long time: the girl’s, and his. Then she dipped the brush, and under both of them, in her own hand — steadier now, a woman’s hand, a physician’s — she wrote the only thing left to add.

All of it.

She closed the notebook and put it back in the chest, and blew out the lamp. Outside, very faintly, from somewhere down by the river, somebody’s child was still singing.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
In another life, Yun Shiyu was a trauma surgeon. In this one she is sixteen, the governor’s daughter in a rainy southern river city, and she has just watched the Emperor’s nephew ride past her balcony.

She does something very foolish to see him again. It turns into six weeks in an army medical tent, three years building a clinic of her own, and a slow, careful love carried mostly in letters — until someone decides to use those letters against them both.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a slow, gentle romance, but some chapters include:

• Battle wounds and field surgery, described from a physician’s point of view

• A near-drowning and an attempted murder (The Riverbank)

• A dislocated shoulder put back in, and a fever (The River Doctor)

• A difficult childbirth, not graphic (A Lamp for the Midwife)

• Grief and fear while a loved one is missing

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I started this one because I wanted a romance where two people fall in love by watching each other be good at their work. She stitches his arm. He reads her reports at night. Nobody says anything for a very long time, and somehow everybody around them notices anyway.

He isn’t cold. He’s careful. She isn’t quiet. She’s honest. That’s most of the story, really.

It ran longer than I planned. I kept thinking they were nearly there and then one of them would write another letter. Thank you for waiting with them all the way to the end.
